Multipole splats for optimized and inverted effective potentials

Matija Medvidović Email: mmedvidovic@ethz.ch Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zürich, 8093 Zürich, Switzerland    Angel Rubio Affiliation: Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter, Luruper Chaussee 149, 22761 Hamburg, Germany Affiliation: Center for Computational Quantum Physics, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA Affiliation: Initiative for Computational Catalysis, Flatiron Institute, 162 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10010, USA    Juan Carrasquilla Affiliation: Institute for Theoretical Physics, ETH Zürich, 8093 Zürich, Switzerland
September 22, 2026
Abstract

In modern density functional theory, effective Hamiltonians are constructed to reproduce densities and forces of electrons at equilibrium. However, their nonlocal potentials leave systematic errors in spectral properties and real-time dynamics. Access to local optimized or inverted effective potentials would remove this limitation, but the numerical fragility in finite orbital bases has long prevented their wide adoption. Here, we introduce multipole splats, a class of trial potentials that carry the correct asymptotic decay required to support the unoccupied spectrum. By connecting the computation of effective potentials to variational and supervised variants of Hamiltonian learning, we recast both problems as stable nonlinear optimization formulated directly in standard orbital basis sets and applicable to any hybrid functional approximation. The resulting solver allows us to resolve spatial profiles of exchange-correlation potential errors during molecular dissociation and accurately reconstruct key excited states without empirical asymptotic corrections. We also show the deviation from the ionization potential theorem for different exchange-correlation approximations on a dataset of molecular systems. Multipole splats extract insights from established approximations and provide capacity for robust dataset generation for downstream processing and learning.

Introduction

Density functional theory (DFT) has offered controlled approximations of many-electron phenomena in molecular and condensed matter systems for decades. Large parts of downstream computational science see DFT as the only interface with quantum phenomena. Materials science [1], quantum chemistry [2, 3], and biology [4] all rely on the underlying effective single-electron description [5, 6] supplied by DFT solvers. This role as a methodological bottleneck has been tightened by the recent developments in data-driven science supported by artificial intelligence (AI), where DFT is used as a data factory for models of quantum matter [7, 8].

While exact in theory, the Kohn-Sham (KS) [6] approach suffers from well-catalogued limitations of approximate exchange-correlation (XC) functionals and finite basis sets [3, 9, 10]. To mitigate self-interaction errors and model thermochemistry, modern generalized Kohn-Sham (GKS) functionals [11, 12] mix in fractions of orbital-dependent exact exchange. The local multiplicative KS potential is replaced by a nonlocal operator, hiding real-space force fields, spectral lines, and the guarantees of KS theorems.

Optimized effective potentials (OEP) [13] restore the true independent-electron physics based on local potentials. The OEP is the multiplicative local potential whose orbitals minimize the total variational GKS energy. In the inverse Kohn-Sham (IKS) problem [14], a local potential is recovered from target density data. In the original formulation [15, 16], evaluating the OEP required inverting the KS response function, which is strongly ill-conditioned in finite basis sets because small response eigenvalues amplify numerical noise and can generate oscillatory, unphysical potentials [17, 18, 9]. Regardless, potentials are most commonly represented as linear combinations of auxiliary basis functions [20, 21, 18, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 9, 27, 10] or replaced by semi-analytical approximations [8, 7, 13, 31, 32]. The data-driven IKS uses physical objectives like the Wu-Yang (WY) [3] or the Zhao-Morrison-Parr [34] functionals but faces the same finite-basis expressivity problem.

The OEP and IKS technical debt is still growing, as accurate potential data is needed at larger scales. Precise IKS potentials are natural targets for machine-learned XC functionals [35] and force fields [7] through the Hellmann-Feynman theorem [9]. Modern calculations with neural quantum states (NQS) [36, 37, 38] produce precise densities uniquely positioned to inform XC functional design through inversion. Reference data errors propagate into machine-learned XC functionals and force fields, affecting downstream predictions.

Time-dependent DFT (TD-DFT) [39, 40, 41] inherits the same problem through its sensitivity to the ground-state potential. Coulomb-like potential tails are required to support key excited states [42, 43, 44, 10]. Beyond the linear response regime, numerical problems are further amplified [45]. In both the data-driven and spectral settings, solver accuracy is a real limitation.

We bypass this inversion by unifying OEP and IKS as Hamiltonian learning problems over parameterized trial potentials. Calculations are reframed as explicitly nonlinear optimization tasks, with a variational energy loss in the OEP case and a quantum density-matching loss in the IKS case, as shown on Figure 1. The KS eigensolver and first-order perturbation theory are connected into a differentiable solver enabling end-to-end optimization. Practical numerical stability is achieved by avoiding ill-conditioned inversions and supplemented by a physics-informed regularizer designed to select a smooth potential.

Trial potentials are built from multipole splats, a superposition of floating Gaussian monopoles and dipoles with optimizable charges, positions, and widths. The potential is modeled as a Coulomb field of a fictitious charge distribution, making it a natural solver output and exactly guaranteeing asymptotic decay vxc≃−γ/rv_{\text{xc}}\simeq\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}} at all times. Asymptotics are built in as a natural constraint rather than left to emerge. Multipole splats inherit tools from Gaussian splats [46], a now-standard method in computer vision for complex three-dimensional scene reconstruction as clouds of floating Gaussians optimized through their projections (splats). We generalize splatting from pixel space to the atomic orbital basis, exploiting standard Gaussian integral technology and enabling reuse of standard quantum chemistry integral routines. Gaussian splats have recently been used to predict electronic densities from data [47, 48].

The WY functional [3, 14] is a standard objective for IKS inversion. To establish a connection between IKS and statistical learning theory, we show that maximizing the WY functional corresponds to relative entropy minimization at zero temperature. The Kohn-Sham state belongs to a quantum exponential family [49, 50], with the potential as its natural parameter and the density as its sufficient statistic. In that formalism, minimizing the quantum relative entropy over admissible potentials is a maximum-likelihood [51, 52] fit that matches the KS density to the target density. Retaining finite β\beta gives the finite-temperature objective derived in Methods.

Here, we show real-space signatures of modern hybrid XC approximations for molecular systems, using multipole splats. We resolve XC potential errors in molecular dissociation by comparing OEPs against IKS reference potentials from coupled-cluster calculations with singles, doubles and perturbative triples (CCSD(T)). These comparisons probe one-electron cancellation, asymmetric dissociation and bond breaking, separating molecular-region errors from asymptotic behavior. We also recover OEP KS gaps and highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) eigenvalues across a dataset of neutral molecular systems, demonstrating access to Rydberg states supported by the −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} exact-exchange (EXX) multipole splat potential without empirical asymptotic corrections. The OEP gap is systematically below the GKS gap, exposing the spectral redistribution associated with localizing the potential. Finally, we compute OEP exchange source densities for larger π\pi-conjugated molecules, directly mapping out electronic delocalization at the scale of ∼70\sim 70 electrons. These results reveal real-space fingerprints of modern exchange-correlation tradeoffs without inverting the KS response.

Results

Multipole splats and direct optimization

The effective potential is the central quantity in Kohn-Sham [5, 6] density functional theory. For NN interacting electrons, a new non-interacting system is constructed such that the two electronic densities nn match. Surrogate KS electrons are described by KS orbitals ϕ={ϕ1,…,ϕN}\phi=\{\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{N}\}. Therefore, we need to find a single-particle potential vv such that the orbitals that solve

(−12∇2+v(𝐫))ϕk(𝐫)=ϵkϕk(𝐫)\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\laplacian+v({\mathbf{r}})\right)\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}})=\epsilon_{k}\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}}) (1)

minimize the total energy functional E⁡[ϕ]E[\phi] [3].

To reinterpret orbital-dependent GKS functionals in the KS language, we need computationally efficient access to optimized effective potentials for orbital-dependent functionals. The OEP is defined as the multiplicative local potential yielding orbitals (via Equation 1) with minimal energy

vOEP=argminvEGKS​[ϕ⁡[v]],v_{\text{OEP}}=\argmin_{v}E_{\text{GKS}}[\phi[v]]\;, (2)

for a given GKS total energy functional EGKSE_{\text{GKS}}.

Alternatively, the exact KS potential can be reconstructed from the exact electronic density n0n_{0} in a data-driven way, bypassing human-designed XC functional approximations. In the inverse Kohn-Sham formalism [14], we construct the potential through density matching,

vIKS=argminv𝒟​[n⁡[v],n0],v_{\text{IKS}}=\argmin_{v}\mathcal{D}[n[v],n_{0}]\;, (3)

where n⁡[v]n[v] is the density built from the solutions of Equation 1 and 𝒟⁡[⋅,⋅]\mathcal{D}[\cdot,\cdot] is a measure of functional divergence between normalized densities.

The IKS potential and the OEP share a common language in Equations 2 and 3. We propose a unified approach to effective KS potential optimization in IKS and OEP frameworks. We view IKS as a data-driven density matching problem and the OEP as a variational energy optimization problem, as outlined in Figure 1. Access to precise OEPs and IKS restores a local KS representation while maintaining the accuracy of higher levels of theory.

Building on Refs. [20, 3], we view the problem of finding the effective potentials through the lens of nonlinear potential optimization in Equations 2 and 3. Orbitals ϕ⁡[v]\phi[v] can be viewed as implicitly parameterized by the potential vv itself through Equation 1. Solving Equation 1 with a variational potential v=vθv=v_{\theta} defines the trial orbitals ϕθ\phi_{\theta}. Parameters θ\theta are directly optimized. Crucially, our approach does not assume a linear potential expansion using an auxiliary basis. The parameterization vθv_{\theta} is completely free. Below, we introduce a physics-informed trial potential that algebraically enforces known asymptotic decay.

Trial potentials must be constrained by known OEP boundary conditions. For neutral molecules and atoms, exact OEPs decay as v≃−1/rv\simeq\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}}, dominated by the exchange component at long ranges. This decay admits an interpretation of the XC component as a Coulomb potential of an auxiliary charge distribution nxc​(𝐫)n_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}}) through the Poisson equation

∇2vxc​(𝐫)=−4​π​nxc​(𝐫).\laplacian v_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}})=-4\pi\,n_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}})\;. (4)

The asymptotic boundary condition is then equivalent to the normalization condition

∫d3𝐫​nxc​(𝐫)=−1,\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;n_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}})=-1\;, (5)

setting the first term in the multipole expansion of the total XC potential. Therefore, the total effective charge density n+nxcn+n_{\text{xc}} can be seen as the electrostatic source density of the electronic effective potential, including all exchange and correlation effects [9], and must integrate to N−1N-1. We exploit the bulk-boundary correspondence established by Equations 4 and 5 to enforce asymptotic conditions.

Some hybrid XC functional approximations use a fraction γ<1\gamma<1 of exact exchange. Because exchange effects define the long-range behavior, the asymptotic decay of the XC potential is then modified to vxc≃−γ/rv_{\text{xc}}\simeq\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}}, and the corresponding nxcn_{\text{xc}} from Equation 5 is required to normalize to −γ-\gamma.

For molecular systems studied in this work, we use a real-space trial potential

vθ​(𝐫)=vext​(𝐫)+vFA​(𝐫)+vMS(θ)​(𝐫),v_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}})=v_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})+v_{\text{FA}}({\mathbf{r}})+{v}_{\text{MS}}^{(\theta)}({\mathbf{r}})\,, (6)

where vextv_{\text{ext}} is the fixed background potential and vFAv_{\text{FA}} is the Fermi-Amaldi (FA) [3] potential generated by a fixed reference density. The final term in Equation 6 is the multipole splat potential vMSv_{\text{MS}}, with free parameters θ\theta. Because the FA term in Equation 6 already carries the correct asymptotic decay, the main role of vMSv_{\text{MS}} is to correct the bulk.

The multipole splat term vMSv_{\text{MS}} is represented as a Coulomb potential of a parametrized charge distribution nMSn_{\text{MS}}. The distribution nMSn_{\text{MS}} is modeled as a superposition of many floating normalized Gaussian monopoles and dipoles with optimizable charges, dipole moments, as well as centers and widths. Each Gaussian charge distribution ρk\rho_{k} generates a known analytic electrostatic potential vkv_{k} by Gauss’ theorem, ensuring that ∇2vk=−4​π​ρk\laplacian v_{k}=-4\pi\rho_{k}. Optimization details and precise functional forms of ρk\rho_{k} and vkv_{k} are provided in Methods.

The target asymptotic boundary condition vxc≃−γ/rv_{\text{xc}}\simeq\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}} is controlled by the total charge QMSQ_{\text{MS}} in the multipole splat cloud. After subtracting the Hartree contribution vHv_{H}, the decay is fixed by the monopole term in the multipole expansion of the trial XC potential vxc=vFA+vMS−vHv_{\text{xc}}=v_{\text{FA}}+v_{\text{MS}}-v_{H}, around the arbitrary origin

vxc​(r)=−1−QMSr+𝒪⁡(1r2),v_{\text{xc}}(r)=-\frac{1-Q_{\text{MS}}}{r}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{r^{2}}\right)\;, (7)

with r=|𝐫|r=|\mathbf{r}|. This is the reason multipole splats are parameterized to satisfy the exact sum rule constraint

QMS=1−γ,Q_{\text{MS}}=1-\gamma\;, (8)

at all times, with γ\gamma set to the exact exchange fraction in the given hybrid functional. By building Equation 8 into the parameterization of the multipole splat cloud, the target asymptotic decay is imposed identically for every parameter value visited during optimization.

Local potential and XC source profiles

Generalized Kohn-Sham calculations with global hybrid functionals contain a fixed fraction γ\gamma of exact exchange [11, 12]

EEXX=−12∑k​l∫d3𝐫∫d3𝐫′ϕk∗​(𝐫)​ϕl∗​(𝐫′)​ϕl​(𝐫)​ϕk​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|.E_{\text{EXX}}=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{kl}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{\phi^{*}_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\phi^{*}_{l}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\phi_{l}({\mathbf{r}})\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}\;. (9)

The EXX functional in Equation 9 is defined by its direct dependence on occupied orbitals, requiring the OEP approach to restore the Kohn-Sham framework. We study the EXX-only solutions as well as some of the most popular hybrid functionals – B3LYP [53] and PBE0 [54].

For B3LYP, γ=1/5\gamma=\nicefrac{{1}}{{5}} and for PBE0, γ=1/4\gamma=\nicefrac{{1}}{{4}}. Multipole splat potentials decay with the required −γ/r\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}} because it has been built into the variational potential as a constraint using the sum rule in Equation 8 rather than treating it as an emergent property. An example of the controllable asymptotic decay can be seen in the right panel of Figure 2.

Optimized trial potentials do not differentiate between Hartree, exchange, and correlation contributions, which are commonly separated in DFT literature [3] and codes. We isolate the XC component by subtracting the Hartree background at convergence as

vxc​(𝐫)=vFA​(𝐫)+vMS​(𝐫)−vH​(𝐫),v_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}})=v_{\text{FA}}({\mathbf{r}})+v_{\text{MS}}({\mathbf{r}})-v_{H}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (10)

where vHv_{H} is the Hartree (Coulomb) potential sourced by the converged OEP or IKS density nn.

Multipole splat potentials recover smooth XC potential spatial profiles. In Figure 2, we show the potentials vxcv_{\text{xc}} and their source densities nxcn_{\text{xc}}, defined by Equation 4, as smooth values along the axis of silicon monoxide (SiO) and carbon monoxide (CO). The converged examples display smooth functions with sharp physical features.

Finite-basis numerical noise amplification is absent in the examples, unlike in some OEP and IKS solvers that rely on auxiliary potential basis sets. The XC source density nxcn_{\text{xc}} reflects the atomic inter-shell peak structure of the molecule and is a primary output of the multipole splat optimization. Modeling the source directly and integrating it analytically avoids numerical finite-difference laplacians applied to a grid representation of the potential, which commonly introduce a new dominant source of error by amplifying numerical noise.

The accuracy of a given OEP calculation can be evaluated from its GKS counterpart. We focus on three figures of merit: the HOMO eigenvalue ϵHOMO\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}}, the localization energy Eloc=EOEP−EGKSE_{\text{loc}}=E_{\text{OEP}}-E_{\text{GKS}}, and the density total variation (TV)

𝒟TV=∫d3𝐫​|n⁡(𝐫)−n0​(𝐫)|,\mathcal{D}_{\text{TV}}=\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;\left|n({\mathbf{r}})-n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\right|\;, (11)

with respect to the appropriate reference density n0n_{0} taken from the GKS calculation. For the IKS case, the reference density n0n_{0} is taken directly from an independent CCSD(T) calculation.

The OEP problem can be seen as the GKS optimization under the constraint of having local potentials. Therefore, EOEP≥EGKSE_{\text{OEP}}\geq E_{\text{GKS}} holds in all cases. The difference Eloc≥0E_{\text{loc}}\geq 0 is the energy penalty of localizing the potential. However, numerical values should be compared with caution for two distinct reasons. Firstly, the EGKSE_{\text{GKS}} floor is a non-monotonically moving target for growing finite orbital basis sets. Secondly, mismatched expressivity between finite parameterizations of orbitals and the potential invalidates the Hohenberg-Kohn one-to-one correspondence between potentials and densities. This mismatch can lead to unphysical potentials that minimize the energy at the expense of representation blind spots instead of building real physical features [17, 6, 9]. In practice, low localization energy is a necessary but not sufficient condition for success [9] and has to be supplemented by independent visual and numerical checks.

The OEP density TV should be treated similarly. It should attain low per-electron values but some differences are expected with respect to GKS because energy is being minimized, not density divergence. The IKS case is simpler – lower TV values indicate a closer density match, given a reliable reference density.

Multipole splat potentials achieve milli-Hartree localization energies while maintaining a close match with GKS densities, as measured by the TV. Exact numerical values for both figures of merit can be found in Supplementary Table 4. Physically meaningful potential, source density and spatial TV profiles on Figure 2 demonstrate the absence of numerical problems. Additional potential profiles are shown in Supplementary Figure 4.

Spatially resolved exchange-correlation potential errors

Local OEPs of orbital-dependent XC approximations can be directly compared to precise IKS references. The multipole splat solver provides both ingredients. In this section, we compare hybrid potentials against the IKS potential obtained from a CCSD(T) density. We define the spatially resolved XC potential error as

Δ​vxcF​(𝐫)=vxcF​(𝐫)−vxcIKS​(𝐫),\Delta v_{\text{xc}}^{F}({\mathbf{r}})=v_{\text{xc}}^{F}({\mathbf{r}})-v_{\text{xc}}^{\text{IKS}}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (12)

where F∈{EXX,B3LYP,PBE0}F\in\{\mathrm{EXX},\,\mathrm{B3LYP},\,\mathrm{PBE0}\} denotes the XC functional approximation. All potentials vanish at infinity, fixing their additive constants. We independently subtract each calculation’s own Hartree potential to extract its XC component, as per Equation 10. The comparison includes density relaxation and does not isolate a pure correlation error. The IKS result is treated in a finite multipole splat representation, not an exact continuum potential.

Figure 3 follows these errors during dissociation of H2+\text{H}_{2}^{+}, HeH+\text{HeH}^{+} and H2\text{H}_{2}. The three systems probe one-electron cancellation, asymmetric dissociation and bond breaking. The asymptotic part of the comparison is fixed by construction: subtracting the −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} IKS tail from a hybrid −γ/r\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}} tail gives Δ​vxcF≃(1−γ)/r\Delta v_{\text{xc}}^{F}\simeq\nicefrac{{(1-\gamma)}}{{r}}. EXX has no such leading tail error. This constraint does not determine the sign or magnitude of errors within the molecule.

Correlation has to vanish identically in H2+\text{H}_{2}^{+} because it is a single-electron system. Exact exchange cancels the Hartree self-interaction [56] while B3LYP and PBE0 cannot. The EXX error in the left column of Figure 3 is indistinguishable from zero on the plotted scale at every separation. B3LYP and PBE0 show similar error profiles throughout dissociation. Both have negative minima near the nuclei and positive errors in the bond and outer regions. The nuclear minima separate as the bond stretches, leaving a broad positive plateau between them. B3LYP has deeper nuclear minima than PBE0, but the spatial pattern is shared. The one-electron comparison exposes incomplete self-interaction cancellation within the molecule as well as in the asymptotic tail.

The middle column follows HeH+\text{HeH}^{+} toward dissociation into neutral He and a bare proton. This limit tests the tendency of approximate functionals to favor fractional fragment charges [57, 58]. At large separations, the strongest hybrid potential errors remain near the proton: a broad positive feature surrounds a narrow negative minimum. EXX stays closer to the reference in this region. The residual identifies where the potentials disagree, but does not by itself establish a fractional charge or a missing interfragment step. The density near the proton becomes small during dissociation, making the inverted potential there less well constrained.

The right column of Figure 3 shows a different pattern as H2\text{H}_{2} enters the strongly correlated bond-breaking regime. At 1.50​Å1.50\,\mathring{\text{A}}, the hybrid midpoint errors remain positive while the EXX error is negative. At 2.502.50 and 5.00​Å5.00\,\mathring{\text{A}}, all three approximations underestimate the reference XC potential at the midpoint and overestimate it in the flanking regions near the nuclei. The midpoint structure is therefore too low relative to its surroundings. B3LYP and PBE0 reduce both the midpoint deficit and the flanking excesses relative to EXX at these larger separations, but do not remove them. In these hybrids, reduced bond-region errors coexist with an asymptotic error set by the reduced exact-exchange fraction.

The three dissociations separate asymptotic accuracy from accuracy within the molecular region. EXX agrees with the one-electron reference but develops substantial bond-region errors in stretched H2\text{H}_{2} despite its correct tail. Hybrid corrections reduce some of those errors but introduce others, most clearly in H2+\text{H}_{2}^{+}. The local-potential comparison resolves where any given XC approximation improves agreement with an accurate correlated reference as well as the spatial distribution of errors.

Spectral properties and Rydberg physics

In the Kohn-Sham framework, occupied and unoccupied orbitals are eigenstates of the same local potential. In GKS or Hartree-Fock (HF) theory, the nonlocal exchange operator acts differently on the two subspaces. An electron in a virtual HF orbital would experience the field of all NN electrons instead of N−1N-1. The residual attraction it feels decays exponentially instead of as −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}}. Therefore, the unoccupied spectrum is a probe of local potentials.

The long Coulomb-like tail of the exact KS potential of a neutral atom supports an infinite Rydberg series of orbital eigenvalues converging to zero, the continuum threshold. Their energies follow the form

εn≈−12​(n−μl)2,\varepsilon_{n}\approx-\frac{1}{2(n-\mu_{l})^{2}}\;, (13)

where nn is the principal quantum number and μl\mu_{l} is the quantum-defect [59] associated with angular momentum ll. The quantum defect depends on how far a Rydberg electron penetrates the atomic core – it is large for low-ll states that penetrate the core and approximately vanishes for high-ll states held out by the centrifugal barrier, which see a bare −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} tail and remain hydrogenic.

The left panel of Figure 4 shows the n​sns (l=0l=0) and n​dnd (l=2l=2) Rydberg series of the Ne atom, plotted against 1/(2​n2)\nicefrac{{1}}{{(2n^{2})}} so that a purely hydrogenic series falls on a straight line through the origin. We compare the orbital eigenvalues with experimental excitation energies measured relative to the ionization limit, EnNIST−IPE_{n}^{\text{NIST}}-I_{P} [16], as detailed in Supplementary Note 6. EXX-OEP closely follows the NIST reference levels [16] across both series and principal quantum numbers shown here, with no empirical asymptotic corrections. These unoccupied KS eigenvalues are not many-body excitation energies, but their quantum defects do provide a diagnostic of the local potential. Despite treating exchange exactly, HF does not reproduce the bound series because its virtual orbitals do not see the −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} tail. This comparison demonstrates that the local potential and the correct asymptotics are both necessary ingredients. The hybrid OEP levels are substantially less bound than the reference levels, consistent with their weaker −γ/r\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}} tails. In the complete-basis limit, these tails still support infinitely many bound states [59]. Our results show that some computed levels lie above the continuum threshold when using finite bases.

On the center panel of Figure 4, converged OEP potentials are drawn against radial distance, with each n​sns and n​dnd eigenvalue overlaid as a horizontal line and its classical turning point marked. Each spectral line in the left panel maps directly onto the depth and width of the supporting potential well. The EXX-OEP potential tracks −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} out to 5050 Bohr, while the hybrid potentials remain shallower and approach their imposed −γ/r\nicefrac{{-\gamma}}{{r}} tails.

Resolving Rydberg physics requires diffuse orbital basis functions. We augment the standard basis with additional diffuse Gaussians for the Ne spectrum (see Supplementary Table 3). Multipole splats accommodate the same physics without modification. Parameterized exponents in Supplementary Equation 45 allow splats to describe spatial structure over many length scales while retaining sharp core features. The asymptotic tail is fixed independently by the charge constraint in Equation 8. Fitting Equation 13 to the converged EXX-OEP levels yields μs=1.351\mu_{s}=1.351 and μd=0.006\mu_{d}=0.006, against 1.3311.331 and 0.0120.012 extracted from Ref. [16]. Both series are recovered to within 55 mHa at n=3n=3 by multipole splats from first principles.

Occupied-state spectra are constrained as well. For the exact KS system, the ionization-potential theorem gives ϵHOMO=−IP\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}}=-I_{P} [57], for the molecular ionization potential IPI_{P}. This equality is not exact for the approximate EXX and hybrid functionals studied here, making the ionization potential an independent diagnostic. The upper right panel of Figure 4 compares HOMO eigenvalues against CCSD(T) ionization potentials across 60 molecules in the GW100 [61] dataset, with at most 40 electrons. Orbitals were represented using the aug-cc-pVTZ orbital basis. EXX-OEP tracks the reference closely over the full ∼1\sim 1 Ha range spanned by the dataset, while the hybrids deviate systematically, by an amount that grows as the exact-exchange fraction γ\gamma gets smaller.

Independent numerical benchmarks against real-space EXX-OEP reference eigenvalues [9] are reported in Supplementary Table 1, with methodological details and potential profiles in Supplementary Note 4 and Supplementary Figure 1. Across the five atoms with available references, the mean absolute deviation of the multipole-splat HOMO eigenvalues is 7.17.1 mHa, without enforcing a HOMO condition or introducing any spectral target into the optimization.

The lower right panel of Figure 4 compares OEP and GKS gaps. The OEP gap ΔOEP\Delta_{\text{OEP}} is smaller than the GKS gap ΔGKS\Delta_{\text{GKS}} throughout the dataset. This difference reflects the spectral rearrangement caused by replacing the nonlocal GKS operator with a local multiplicative potential in Equation 1. Among the approximations studied, EXX receives the largest correction. In exact KS theory, the fundamental gap differs from the orbital gap by the XC derivative discontinuity [57, 62, 63]. GKS eigenvalue gaps can incorporate part of this contribution [64, 65]. This provides context for the gap comparison, but the present gap difference alone is not sufficient to estimate the derivative discontinuity. Regardless, these potentials may offer a principled starting point for linear-response TD-DFT, where excitation energies also depend on the XC kernel.

Larger molecular systems

Effective potentials are usually expanded in an auxiliary basis whose balance against the orbital basis has to be maintained by hand [17, 18, 9]. Splats are allocated per occupied orbital (see Supplementary Note 3), so the parameterization needs no per-system tuning.

In this section, we compute EXX OEP potentials for benzene (42 electrons) and naphthalene (68 electrons), shown in Figure 5 on a plane 11 Bohr above the molecular plane, using the cc-pVTZ orbital basis. The potentials resolve π\pi-conjugated systems. For benzene, exchange charge is distributed evenly around the ring, the real-space signature of complete π\pi delocalization. Splats are initialized symmetrically with respect to the molecular point group and optimized without symmetry constraints. The converged exchange potential source density preserves the six-fold symmetry. On the other hand, naphthalene breaks the pattern. The map separates the peripheral carbons from the ring-fusion region, consistent with the bond inequivalence that distinguishes naphthalene from benzene and absent from the smaller molecule.

Accuracy does not degrade with system size for these examples, provided that enough splats are used. The right column of Figure 5 shows the pointwise density deviation from the GKS reference staying below 0.0050.005 a.u. across both molecules, with nodal lines where the two densities cross appearing as sharp minima. Similar to a standard GKS calculation, the per-step cost of direct potential optimization is dominated by the integral evaluation and eigendecomposition steps.

Discussion

Effective single-electron potentials are naturally defined as solutions to constrained optimization problems. Their treatment as implicit density functionals within the self-consistent field (SCF) framework [15, 16, 13] commonly requires an ill-conditioned inversion of the density response operator whose regularization has occupied the field for decades [17, 18, 9], blocking access to force fields and spectra furnished by multiplicative potentials. In Methods, we formulate OEP and IKS problems as nonlinear optimization [20, 3] over trial potentials, replacing response inversion with first-order optimization. We explore this tradeoff and argue that modern nonlinear optimization has become a practical tool for reliable computation of effective potentials.

Multipole splats have been proposed as a natural and expressive choice for the nonlinear trial potential parameterization, with exact asymptotics built in and guaranteed. They have been inspired by modern methods for three-dimensional scene reconstruction in computer vision [46]. A robust first-order gradient-based optimizer has been borrowed from the AI literature. These ingredients are ready to be used as self-contained OEP and IKS solvers, removing the need to hand-tune auxiliary bases and asymptotic corrections, and giving functional designers more spatial and geometrical diagnostics.

To complete the IKS theory frame, we have shown that KS potential inversion through WY [3] maximization is equivalent to maximum-likelihood estimation [51] of the full equilibrium KS density operator using the density as the sufficient statistic [50]. This theoretical connection roots the well-known mathematical properties and stability of the WY functional [66] in statistical learning theory [49] and allows us to extend the WY inversion protocol to finite-temperature states. These connections position IKS as a tool for building the next generation of electronic structure datasets.

Comparing self-consistent XC potentials against IKS references from the same solver offers real-space resolution of approximate functional errors [58]. The dissociation profiles show that correct asymptotics do not guarantee accuracy within the molecule. Hybrids reduce some bond-region errors in stretched H2\text{H}_{2} despite their incorrect tails. The exact exchange potential closely follows reference Rydberg series and quantum defects [16], showing the role of both locality and asymptotic decay in the unoccupied KS spectrum. The same optimization produces accurate HOMO eigenvalues across the GW100 subset [61] and exposes the gap redistribution associated with replacing a nonlocal operator by a local potential [57, 64], while exchange source densities for π\pi-conjugated molecules demonstrate robust results at the scale of tens of electrons.

Some numerical scaffolding is still required. Non-uniqueness caused by finite orbital and potential representations is the main obstacle to completely unregularized determination of OEPs. This is a well-known consequence of Hohenberg-Kohn [5] theorems breaking in finite bases [17, 6]. In practice, regularization is effective in mitigating this problem, but it cannot be removed completely. Enforcing HOMO energy conditions can be added as extra regularization [9]. Additionally, first-order optimization takes many iterations to converge and analytic three-center integral evaluation remains CPU-bound. Immediate next steps are natural gradient optimization [67] and a GPU-resident integral engine, which would remove host-device communication overhead. We expect these extensions to make the execution speed competitive with SCF methods.

Having established a close connection between the KS unoccupied states, the self-interaction error, and potential asymptotics, we plan on using multipole splats with exact asymptotics on functionals that otherwise yield incorrectly decaying potentials, building algebraically constrained adaptive range separation [68]. Enforcing long-range behavior via basis preprocessing has already been shown to meaningfully correct spectral properties in Ref. [10]. The learning setup is agnostic to the theory supplying the energy or the density, opening a route to orbital-dependent correlation functionals whose self-consistent potentials are only now becoming available [69]. When a stationary total-energy functional derived from a self-energy approximation is available, its local OEP can be computed as well. An extension of multipole splats to periodic systems is possible in reciprocal space as well [48]. In addition, direct amortization of the proposed solvers can be achieved by predicting splat parameters directly [47] using modern neural networks. Amortization may reduce the need to run independent calculations during TD-DFT evolution by effectively storing interpolated results in neural network parameters [70]. A model predicting splat parameters inherits the asymptotic decay by construction.

Inverse Kohn-Sham potentials can also be retrieved from state-of-the-art synthetic and experimental data using the proposed generalization of the finite-temperature [4] WY objective. The exact convex loss gradient only needs point-wise density residuals. Therefore, different approaches like NQS or cold atom experiments [72, 73], where sampling is much easier than direct evaluation, are accommodated with no reformulation. This framework steps away from XC functional approximations where data is available.

In practice, the numerical reliability of multipole splat optimization is a prerequisite both for studies of exchange-correlation physics and for the AI training that functional development requires. We expect the framework and its natural extensions to be productive on both sides of this correspondence.

Methods

Local and nonlocal potentials

The Kohn-Sham potential vv in Equation 1 is traditionally decomposed as v=vext+vH+vxcv=v_{\text{ext}}+v_{H}+v_{\text{xc}}, where vextv_{\text{ext}} is the external potential, vHv_{H} is the classical Coulomb (Hartree) contribution, and vxcv_{\text{xc}} is the exchange-correlation component. The correlated character of the final solution is built in through the density dependence of the XC potential, modeled by the XC energy functional Exc​[n]E_{\text{xc}}[n] as vxc=𝛿Exc𝛿nv_{\text{xc}}=\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{n}. Densities calculated from solutions to Equation 1 are called vv-representable because they are compatible with a multiplicative scalar potential vv.

The exact XC potential comes with theoretical guarantees. The exact highest occupied molecular orbital KS eigenvalue is identified with the negative ionization potential of the molecule [57], ϵHOMO=−IP\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}}=-I_{P}. The XC potential decays as vxc≃−1/rv_{\text{xc}}\simeq-\nicefrac{{1}}{{r}} asymptotically as r→∞r\rightarrow\infty and is free from the self-interaction error. SIE cancelation is crucial for localized states, transition metal oxides, as well as time-dependent and response properties in general.

Approximate XC energy functionals and finite basis expansions [9] spoil these exact guarantees in practical calculations. When approximate XC energy functionals are modeled as true density functionals, Exc=Exc​[n]E_{\text{xc}}=E_{\text{xc}}[n], potentials can be obtained by direct functional differentiation. However, modern hybrid functionals explicitly depend on orbitals, Exc=Exc​[ϕ]E_{\text{xc}}=E_{\text{xc}}[\phi].

The resulting stationary-point generalized KS equations [12], 𝛿E𝛿ϕ=0\functionalderivative{E}{\phi}=0, include non-local contributions to the potential. For example, hybrid functionals contain a fraction γ\gamma of the nonlocal exact exchange energy, Exc=Eloc​[n]+γ​EEXX​[ϕ]E_{\text{xc}}=E_{\text{loc}}[n]+\gamma E_{\text{EXX}}[\phi]. The GKS orbitals then solve

(−12∇2+vloc(𝐫))ϕk(𝐫)−γ(Kϕ)k(𝐫)=ϵkϕk(𝐫),\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\laplacian+v_{\text{loc}}({\mathbf{r}})\right)\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}})-\gamma(K\phi)_{k}({\mathbf{r}})=\epsilon_{k}\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\,, (14)

where vlocv_{\text{loc}} is the local component of the potential and KK is the nonlocal (orbital-mixing) exchange potential

(K​ϕ)k​(𝐫)=∑l∫d3𝐫′​ϕk​(𝐫′)​ϕl​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|​ϕl​(𝐫)(K\phi)_{k}({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{l}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\phi_{l}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}\phi_{l}({\mathbf{r}}) (15)

formed from occupied KS orbitals. Mathematically, Equation 14 simply admits more solutions than Equation 1, departing from the vv-representable context [13].

If we attempt to compute the KS potential by direct differentiation of an orbital-dependent ExcE_{\text{xc}}, we reach a roadblock. Schematically,

vxc=𝛿Exc​[ϕ]𝛿n=𝛿Exc​[ϕ]𝛿ϕ⋅𝛿ϕ𝛿n.v_{\text{xc}}=\functionalderivative{E_\xc[\phi]}{n}=\functionalderivative{E_\xc[\phi]}{\phi}\cdot\functionalderivative{\phi}{n}\;. (16)

Because the map from occupied orbitals to the density is many-to-one, including the freedom to rotate the occupied orbitals, 𝛿ϕ𝛿n\functionalderivative{\phi}{n} is not uniquely defined without specifying an inverse density-to-potential map and an orbital gauge. In principle, vxcv_{\text{xc}} can be obtained as a solution of a linear system [15, 16, 13]

∫d3𝐫′​χs​(𝐫,𝐫′)​vxc​(𝐫′)=t⁡(𝐫)\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})v_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=t({\mathbf{r}}) (17)

where χs=𝛿n𝛿v\chi_{s}=\functionalderivative{n}{v} is the KS static response function and t=𝛿Exc𝛿vt=\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{v}. However, inversion of Equation 17 is notoriously ill-conditioned in finite basis sets [9, 27], costing accuracy at best and causing uncontrolled numerical instabilities at worst.

Unified framework for optimized and inverted potentials

The KS orbitals remain expressed as a linear combination of suitably chosen basis functions χμ\chi_{\mu} indexed by Greek indices μ\mu

ϕk​(𝐫)=∑μCμ​k​[v]​χμ​(𝐫),\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{\mu}C_{\mu k}[v]\,\chi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (18)

by viewing the linear combination coefficients CC as a functional of the trial potential vv or, equivalently, as a function of any variational parameters θ\theta. Coefficients CC are determined as a solution to Equation 1 in the chosen basis set χμ\chi_{\mu}, giving rise to the standard generalized eigenvalue problem of the form H​C=S​C​ϵHC=SC\epsilon. For non-degenerate eigenvalues, the eigendecomposition in a finite basis is a differentiable mapping H↦(C,ϵ)H\mapsto(C,\epsilon) with gradients given by well-known first-order perturbation theory formulas [74]. For degenerate eigenvalues, we establish a heuristic regularization procedure outlined in Supplementary Note 1, implemented as a custom gradient rule in our differentiable solver.

The effective single-particle Hamiltonian HH is simply the operator

Hθ=−12∇2+vθ,H_{\theta}=-\tfrac{1}{2}\laplacian+v_{\theta}\;, (19)

projected down into the orbital basis χ\chi. The variational potential vθv_{\theta} contributes to the eigenvalue equation as an additive term with its matrix representation

Vμ​ν=∫d3𝐫​vθ​(𝐫)​χμ​(𝐫)​χν​(𝐫).V_{\mu\nu}=\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;v_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}})\,\chi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})\,\chi_{\nu}({\mathbf{r}})\;. (20)

The projection in Equation 20 can be viewed as generalized splatting onto a finite-dimensional basis set. Similar to the Gaussian splatting method in computer vision literature [46], multipole splats are optimized exclusively through their projections onto the orbital basis χ\chi. Despite being optimized through generalized splatting defined in Equation 20, the potential inherits the real-space asymptotic constraints from our multipole splat ansatz introduced below.

For the OEP, we seek to minimize the GKS energy EGKSE_{\text{GKS}} such that ϕ⁡[v]\phi[v] are the vv-representable orbitals implicitly defined by the multiplicative local potential vv in Equation 1. In practice, we optimize the regularized variational energy functional

E⁡(θ)=EGKS​[ϕ⁡[vθ]]+λ​R​[vθ],E(\theta)=E_{\text{GKS}}[\phi[v_{\theta}]]+\lambda\,R[v_{\theta}]\;, (21)

to compute the OEP or the regularized divergence with respect to the reference density n0n_{0}

𝒟⁡(θ)=𝒟⁡[n⁡[vθ],n0]+λ​R​[vθ],\mathcal{D}(\theta)=\mathcal{D}[n[v_{\theta}],n_{0}]+\lambda\,R[v_{\theta}]\;, (22)

with a small positive constant λ\lambda. The regularization term R⁡[v]R[v] in Equations 21 and 22 is chosen to resolve the null-space of different solutions in favor of smoother potentials. Our specific choice of R⁡[v]R[v] is introduced below.

The mapping θ↦E⁡(θ)\theta\mapsto E(\theta) is differentiable because it is built as a composition of differentiable functions. Therefore, optimal variational parameters θ\theta are computed using gradient-based optimization of the total energy functional in Equation 21. Parameter gradients require the evaluation of the orbital response function because

𝛿E𝛿vθ=𝛿E⁡[ϕ]𝛿ϕ⋅𝛿ϕ𝛿vθ.\functionalderivative{E}{v_\theta}=\functionalderivative{E[\phi]}{\phi}\cdot\functionalderivative{\phi}{v_\theta}\;. (23)

The orbital response 𝛿ϕ𝛿v\functionalderivative{\phi}{v} can be obtained through first-order perturbation theory. Crucially, inverting the response function is not required, removing the main source of numerical instabilities in traditional approaches [12]. The internal sum over all unoccupied states can be carried out directly or implicitly through the Sternheimer equation [75].

Inverse Kohn-Sham as supervised Hamiltonian learning

To compute the IKS potential, we start from the quantum Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence or the relative von Neumann entropy. For a reference state ρ^0\hat{\rho}_{0} with density n0n_{0} and the finite-temperature KS Gibbs state ρ^β​[v]\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v], the quantum KL divergence is defined as

𝒟KL(ρ^0∥ρ^β[v])=−Tr⁡(ρ^0​(ln⁡ρ^β​[v]−ln⁡ρ^0))\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\rho}_{0}\parallel\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v])=-\Tr{ \Hat\rho_0 \left( \ln\Hat\rho_\beta[v] - \ln\Hat\rho_0 \right) } (24)

where the two states are taken to have the same expected particle number. Only the reference density n0n_{0} enters the potential-dependent part of Equation 24, so the full reference state does not need to be constructed. In this work, n0n_{0} is obtained using the relaxed CCSD(T) [76], but reference densities could be imported from arbitrary sources.

We show that minimizing the scaled zero-temperature limit of Equation 24 is equivalent to maximizing the WY functional introduced in Ref. [3],

W⁡[v]=Ts​[ϕ⁡[v]]+∫d3𝐫​v​(𝐫)​(n⁡[v]​(𝐫)−n0​(𝐫)),W[v]=T_{s}[\phi[v]]+\int\differential[3]{\rr}v({\mathbf{r}})(n[v]({\mathbf{r}})-n_{0}({\mathbf{r}}))\;, (25)

where Ts​[ϕ]T_{s}[\phi] is the non-interacting kinetic energy. Equations 24 and 25 frame a fundamental result in the IKS theory as a supervised Hamiltonian learning problem. Details can be found in Supplementary Note 1 where we show that

argminvlimβ→∞β−1𝒟KL(ρ^0∥ρ^β[v])=argmaxvW[v].\argmin_{v}\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}\beta^{-1}\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\rho}_{0}\parallel\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v])=\argmax_{v}W[v]\;. (26)

The result in Equation 26 can be used to generalize the WY IKS approach to finite temperatures. In practice, we minimize the regularized loss

𝒟⁡(θ)=−W⁡[vθ]+λ​R​[vθ],\mathcal{D}(\theta)=-W[v_{\theta}]+\lambda\,R[v_{\theta}]\;, (27)

inheriting mathematical properties from the original formulation in Equation 24.

The thermal density operator ρ^β​[v]∝e−β​(H^​[v]−μ​N^)\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v]\propto e^{-\beta(\hat{H}[v]-\mu\hat{N})} belongs to the quantum exponential family [49, 50] for a KS Hamiltonian in Equation 19. The potential vv is a natural parameter and the density nn is the mean parameter (corresponding to a sufficient statistic) of ρ^β\hat{\rho}_{\beta} so that minimizing Equation 24 is maximum-likelihood estimation [51, 52] in that family. Convexity of the log-partition function in the natural parameter is the origin of the convexity of the loss and of the negative semi-definiteness of the KS response χs\chi_{s}, while its derivative yields the density nn. At zero temperature this is precisely the Legendre structure identified by Lieb [66].

Therefore, the WY functional is concave in the variational potential, while the negative WY loss used in Equation 27 is convex in the potential. From Equation 25, gradients of the WY functional simply evaluate to the density residual

𝛿W𝛿v=n⁡[v]−n0,\functionalderivative{W}{v}=n[v]-n_{0}\;, (28)

vanishing exactly when n⁡[v]=n0n[v]=n_{0}. Therefore, exploiting n0n_{0} allows us to bypass the calculation of the unoccupied states appearing in gradients of Equation 21.

Practical optimization of multipole splats

We use a real-space trial potential introduced in Equation 6 for an isolated molecule with AA atoms with charges ZaZ_{a} at coordinates 𝐑a{\mathbf{R}}_{a} (a=1,…,Aa=1,\,\ldots,\,A) and NN electrons. The fixed background nuclear Coulomb contribution is vext(𝐫)=−∑aZ∕a∕|∕𝐫∕−∕𝐑∕a∕|v_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})=-\sum_{a}\ifrac{Z_{a}}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{R}}_{a}|} and

vFA​(𝐫)=N−1N​∫d3𝐫′​nref​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|v_{\text{FA}}({\mathbf{r}})=\frac{N-1}{N}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\,\frac{n_{\text{ref}}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|} (29)

is the Fermi-Amaldi potential generated by a fixed reference density nrefn_{\text{ref}}. The final term in Equation 6 is the multipole splat potential vMSv_{\text{MS}}, detailed below.

The multipole splat source density nMSn_{\text{MS}} models the contribution to nxcn_{\text{xc}} on top of nrefn_{\text{ref}} as

nMS​(𝐫)=∑k=1N1qk​ρk​(𝐫)−∑k=1N2𝐩k⋅∇ρk​(𝐫),n_{\text{MS}}({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{1}}q_{k}\rho_{k}({\mathbf{r}})-\sum_{k=1}^{N_{2}}\mathbf{p}_{k}\cdot\gradient\rho_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (30)

with charges qkq_{k} and dipole moments 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k}, respectively. In Equation 30, sources ρk\rho_{k} are normalized Gaussians centered at 𝐚k\mathbf{a}_{k} with finite widths set by exponents αk\alpha_{k}. Charge densities in Equation 30 source a parameterized electrostatic potential given by

vMS​(𝐫)=∑k=1N1qk​vk​(𝐫)−∑k=1N2𝐩k⋅∇vk​(𝐫),v_{\text{MS}}({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{k=1}^{N_{1}}q_{k}v_{k}({\mathbf{r}})-\sum_{k=1}^{N_{2}}\mathbf{p}_{k}\cdot\gradient v_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (31)

making up the total multipole splat potential. Each elementary multipole source ρk\rho_{k} generates an analytical electrostatic potential vkv_{k}, allowing us to model the source density and the resulting potential using the same parameters θ\theta. Precise functional forms of ρk\rho_{k} and vkv_{k} have been listed in Table 1.

If all individual ρk\rho_{k} are normalized to unity, the total charge of the N1N_{1} monopoles is QMS=∑kqkQ_{\text{MS}}=\sum_{k}q_{k}. Practically, we define unconstrained weights wkw_{k} and set

qk=wk−1N1​∑j=1N1wj+1−γN1q_{k}=w_{k}-\frac{1}{N_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{1}}w_{j}+\frac{1-\gamma}{N_{1}} (32)

for a functional that uses an exact exchange fraction γ\gamma. Equation 32 enforces the sum rule QMS=∑kqk=1−γQ_{\text{MS}}=\sum_{k}q_{k}=1-\gamma at all times, with controllable γ\gamma built into the parameterization. Values of wkw_{k} are unconstrained and can be optimized freely.

Physically, the variational potential is constrained to have the correct asymptotics by requiring the monopole term to carry a prescribed excess charge. Neutral multipole clouds model the exact KS potential. Charge can be added manually to model non-unit fractions of exact exchange, intentionally altering the asymptotic decay.

Variational parameters θ\theta in Equation 6 contain all of the monopole and dipole positions, exponents, charges and dipole moments,

θ={wk,αk,𝐚k}k=1N1∪{𝐩k,αk,𝐚k}k=1N2,\theta=\Big\{w_{k},\alpha_{k},\mathbf{a}_{k}\Big\}_{k=1}^{N_{1}}\;\cup\;\Big\{\mathbf{p}_{k},\alpha_{k},\mathbf{a}_{k}\Big\}_{k=1}^{N_{2}}\;, (33)

adding up to P=5​N1+7​N2P=5N_{1}+7N_{2} variational parameters. Anisotropic Gaussians [46] and optimizable quadrupoles or even higher floating multipoles could be included for additional expressivity in specific applications. We use the standard first-order gradient-based optimizer Adamax [77] to numerically optimize all of the parameters simultaneously. Crucially, Adamax is a first-order optimizer and never constructs or attempts to approximate or invert the ill-conditioned parameter Hessian matrix [20]. All calculations use a restricted spatial-orbital convention, with occupations in {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}. All CCSD(T) reference densities are computed in the same orbital basis as the inversion. Complete hyperparameter settings for every calculation reported above are given in Supplementary Table 2. See Supplementary Note 6 for details.

There is no Coulomb singularity in Equation 31. Pure point monopoles and dipoles have delta-function source densities q​δ​(𝐫−𝐚)q\delta({\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{a}) and −𝐩⋅∇δ(𝐫−𝐚)-\mathbf{p}\cdot\gradient\delta({\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{a}), respectively, giving rise to singular Coulomb potentials. We bypass numerical instabilities associated with delta functions by modeling our sources as finite-width Gaussians defined in Table 1, keeping both densities and potentials analytic. Formally, we can recover the delta function as a limit limα→∞ρ⁡(𝐫)=δ⁡(𝐫−𝐚)\lim_{\alpha\to\infty}\rho({\mathbf{r}})=\delta({\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{a}).

Other parameters in Equation 33 are not constrained by physics. Regardless, we do parameterize the multipole positions 𝐚k\mathbf{a}_{k} and the exponents in a way that constrains their magnitude. For details on parameterization and optimization, see Supplementary Note 3.

Setting ∑kqk=0\sum_{k}q_{k}=0 is possible even for global hybrids and pure density XC functionals, forcing the optimization to converge to a smooth interpolation between the bulk and the exact −1/r-\nicefrac{{1}}{{r}} asymptotic decay, instead of intentionally removing exact constraints to facilitate known functional deficiencies. We leave this form of adaptive range separation for future work.

Each monopole or dipole is a floating ss or pp orbital. As a consequence, potential matrix elements that contribute to the generalized splatting eigenvalue problem in Equation 20 can be evaluated analytically. Combining Equation 20 and the functional forms of multipole splats given in Table 1, we have

Vμ​ν(1)=∑kqk​∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​χμ​(𝐫)​χν​(𝐫)​ρk​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|V^{(1)}_{\mu\nu}=\sum_{k}q_{k}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{\chi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})\chi_{\nu}({\mathbf{r}})\rho_{k}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|} (34)

for the monopole term. A nearly identical expression can be written down for the dipole term, by replacing qkρk→−𝐩⋅∇ρkq_{k}\rho_{k}\rightarrow-\mathbf{p}\cdot\gradient\rho_{k}. Both the integral in Equation 34 and its dipole equivalent can be evaluated using the standard three-center Gaussian integral routines commonly used for density fitting. No grid integration is required. However, we found that evaluating Equation 20 on a numerical quadrature grid yielded almost identical accuracy in our experiments.

Regularization

We use a physics-informed regularization term R⁡[v]R[v] [18, 22, 26, 78] in Equations 21 and 27. Minimizing the expression

R⁡[v]=18​π​∫d3𝐫​|∇v​(𝐫)−∇v0​(𝐫)|2R[v]=\frac{1}{8\pi}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\,\left|\gradient v({\mathbf{r}})-\gradient v_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\right|^{2} (35)

enforces the smoothness bias by force matching [79] against a fixed reference potential v0v_{0}. Intuitively, adding the regularization term resolves the null space of near-degenerate OEP solutions in favor of smoother potentials.

In the case of multipole splat trial potentials, the regularization integral in Equation 35 is carried out against the reference potential v0=vext+vFAv_{0}=v_{\text{ext}}+v_{\text{FA}}, resulting in the electrostatic energy of the multipole splat contribution alone,

R⁡[vθ]=\displaystyle R[v_{\theta}]= 18​π​∫d3𝐫​|∇vMS​(𝐫)|2\displaystyle\frac{1}{8\pi}\int\differential[3]{\rr}|\gradient v_{\text{MS}}({\mathbf{r}})|^{2} (36)
=\displaystyle= 12​∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​nMS​(𝐫)​nMS​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|.\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{n_{\text{MS}}({\mathbf{r}})n_{\text{MS}}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}\;. (37)

The Coulomb energy in Equation 37 can be evaluated analytically as well, completely bypassing grid integration of trial potentials in the entire optimization loop.

Regularization defined in Equation 35 is not required for numerical convergence. A small positive constant λ\lambda is used to select a visually appealing potential between all of the degenerate solutions with almost identical energies. This near-degeneracy is shown to correspond to the null space of the KS response function in Supplementary Note 2, responsible for numerical problems in traditional solvers that rely on inversion. Visually, the optimization procedure produces potentials with correct large-scale physical features even at λ→0\lambda\rightarrow 0 (see Supplementary Note 5 and Supplementary Figure 2 and Supplementary Figure 3). From the physical point of view, regularization biases the optimization towards solutions with electric fields (or forces) 𝐄=−∇v\mathbf{E}=-\gradient v matching those of the background v0v_{0}.

In operator form, the total energy functional Hessian ℋ\mathcal{H} at the optimum takes the form ℋ=−χs​χ−1​χs\mathcal{H}=-\chi_{s}\chi^{-1}\chi_{s}, where χ=𝛿n𝛿vext\chi=\functionalderivative{n}{v_\ext} is the density response operator. Therefore, the Hessian shares the null space with the KS response χs\chi_{s}, manifesting as flat directions at the optimum in the energy landscape E⁡[v]E[v]. The effect of the additive regularizer in Equation 35 is to add its own positive definite Hessian ℋreg=−14​π∇2\mathcal{H}_{\text{reg}}=-\tfrac{1}{4\pi}\laplacian to that of the total energy or the quantum KL divergence, making the total Hessian strictly positive definite, up to constant shifts. The full derivation and additional details can be found in Supplementary Note 2.

Data availability

The converged potentials, source densities, orbital coefficients and spectra supporting the findings of this study, together with the molecular geometries and reference densities used as inputs, are available upon reasonable request from the corresponding author. The Ne I reference term values are available from the NIST Atomic Spectra Database [16], and the GW100 reference ionization potentials from Ref. [61].

Code availability

All simulations were performed using the JAX [80] library for array manipulation and automatic differentiation. Equinox [81] was used for model design, and Optax for optimization. Data was post-processed using NumPy [82] and SciPy [83]. The plots were produced using the Matplotlib [84] library. The custom code library needed to reproduce the results in this work and explore new ones can be found in the following repository: https://github.com/Matematija/multipole-splats.
