Multipole splats for optimized and inverted effective potentials
Supplementary Information

Supplementary Note 1: Exact gradients

Optimized effective potentials

In the main text, we minimize the total energy functional E⁡[ϕ]E[\phi] as a functional of the orbitals such that the orbitals are compatible with a single-particle multiplicative potential. We define our trial orbitals ϕ=ϕ⁡[v]\phi=\phi[v], thinking of these orbitals as functionals of a trial single-particle potential vv. In other words, the orbitals solve

(−12∇2+v(𝐫))ϕi(𝐫)=ϵiϕi(𝐫),\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}\laplacian+v({\mathbf{r}})\right)\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})=\epsilon_{i}\,\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (1)

for some vv. Following the Kohn-Sham (KS) recipe, we seek to find the vv that minimizes the total density functional theory (DFT) energy EE as a functional of the trial potential vv, vOEP=argminvE​[ϕ⁡[v]]v_{\text{OEP}}=\argmin_{v}E[\phi[v]].

Equation 1 is not the Kohn-Sham equation we are trying to solve but is simply a defining equation for the trial orbitals. We explicitly parameterize the potential v=vθv=v_{\theta}, requiring us to carry the gradients through the solution of Equation 1 during gradient-based optimization. Assuming real orbitals ϕi​(𝐫)∈ℝ\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\in\mathbbm{R}, and using the chain rule, we expand

∂E∂θa=∑i∫d3𝐫​𝛿E⁡[ϕ]𝛿ϕi∗​(𝐫)​∂ϕi∗​(𝐫)∂θa+c.c.=∑i∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​𝛿E⁡[ϕ]𝛿ϕi∗​(𝐫)​𝛿ϕi∗​(𝐫)𝛿v⁡(𝐫′)​∂v⁡(𝐫′)∂θa+c.c..\partialderivative{E}{\theta_a}=\sum_{i}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\functionalderivative{E [\phi]}{\phi^* _i (\rr)}\partialderivative{\phi^* _i (\rr)}{\theta_a}\;+\;\text{c.c.}=\sum_{i}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\functionalderivative{E [\phi]}{\phi^* _i (\rr)}\functionalderivative{\phi^* _i (\rr)}{v (\rr')}\partialderivative{v(\rr')}{\theta_a}\;+\;\text{c.c.}\;. (2)

In Equation 2, the chain rule application results in the product of three derivative factors. The first term results in the generally orbital-dependent DFT single-particle Hamiltonian. As an example, for hybrid functionals with an exact-exchange fraction γ\gamma, we have

𝛿E⁡[ϕ]𝛿ϕi∗​(𝐫)=(𝐇^ϕ)i(𝐫)=[−12∇2+vext(𝐫)+vH(𝐫)+vxc(loc)(𝐫)]ϕi(𝐫)−γ∑jKi​j(𝐫)ϕj(𝐫),\functionalderivative{E [\phi]}{\phi^* _i (\rr)}=(\hat{\mathbf{H}}\,\phi)_{i}({\mathbf{r}})=\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\laplacian+v_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})+v_{H}({\mathbf{r}})+v_{\text{xc}}^{(\text{loc})}({\mathbf{r}})\right]\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})-\gamma\sum_{j}K_{ij}({\mathbf{r}})\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (3)

where 𝐇^=𝐇^​[ϕ]\hat{\mathbf{H}}=\hat{\mathbf{H}}[\phi] is the effective generalized Kohn-Sham (GKS) Hamiltonian operator, comprised of the external potential vextv_{\text{ext}}, the local exchange-correlation (XC) contribution vxc(loc)v_{\text{xc}}^{(\text{loc})}, and the standard direct (Coulomb or Hartree) term and exchange (Fock) terms,

vH​(𝐫)=∫d3𝐫′​n⁡(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|,Ki​j​(𝐫)=∫d3𝐫′​ϕi​(𝐫′)​ϕj∗​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|.v_{H}({\mathbf{r}})=\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{n({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}\;,\qquad K_{ij}({\mathbf{r}})=\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\phi^{*}_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}\;. (4)

The orbital response factor 𝛿ϕ𝛿v\functionalderivative{\phi}{v} is given by first-order perturbation theory:

𝛿ϕi​(𝐫)𝛿v⁡(𝐫′)=∑j≠iϕj​(𝐫)​ϕj∗​(𝐫′)ϵi−ϵj​ϕi​(𝐫′)\functionalderivative{\phi_i (\rr)}{v (\rr')}=\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}})\phi^{*}_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}}\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}) (5)

We arrive at the final expression

∂E∂θa=\displaystyle\partialderivative{E}{\theta_a}= ∑i∑j≠i∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​(𝐇^​ϕ)i​(𝐫)​ϕj∗​(𝐫)​ϕj​(𝐫′)ϵi−ϵj​ϕi∗​(𝐫′)​∂v⁡(𝐫′)∂θa+c.c.\displaystyle\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}(\hat{\mathbf{H}}\,\phi)_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\frac{\phi^{*}_{j}({\mathbf{r}})\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}}\phi^{*}_{i}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\partialderivative{v(\rr')}{\theta_a}+\;\text{c.c.} (6)
=\displaystyle= ∑i∑j≠i[∫d3𝐫​ϕj∗​(𝐫)​𝐇^​ϕi​(𝐫)]​1ϵi−ϵj​[∫d3𝐫′​ϕi∗​(𝐫′)​∂v⁡(𝐫′)∂θa​ϕj​(𝐫′)]+c.c.\displaystyle\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\left[\int\differential[3]{\rr}\phi^{*}_{j}({\mathbf{r}})\hat{\mathbf{H}}\;\phi_{i}({\mathbf{r}})\right]\frac{1}{\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}}\left[\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\phi^{*}_{i}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\partialderivative{v(\rr')}{\theta_a}\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\right]+\;\text{c.c.} (7)
=\displaystyle= ∑i∑j≠iHi​j​Gi​jϵi−ϵj+c.c.\displaystyle\sum_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\frac{H_{ij}G_{ij}}{\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}}+\;\text{c.c.} (8)

where Hi​j=⟨ϕi|​𝐇​|ϕj⟩H_{ij}=\bra{\phi_i}\mathbf{H}\ket{\phi_j} are the GKS Hamiltonian matrix elements in the optimized effective potential (OEP) orbital basis and

Gi​ja=∫d3𝐫′​ϕi∗​(𝐫′)​∂v⁡(𝐫′)∂θa​ϕj​(𝐫′)=⟨ϕi|​𝐆^a​|ϕj⟩G^{a}_{ij}=\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\phi^{*}_{i}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\partialderivative{v(\rr')}{\theta_a}\phi_{j}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\bra{\phi_i}\hat{\mathbf{G}}^{a}\ket{\phi_j} (9)

can be understood as matrix elements of a potential gradient operator. The gradient expression in Equation 6 has several advantages over traditional approaches. Firstly, it is numerically stable to evaluate unless ϵi≈ϵj\epsilon_{i}\approx\epsilon_{j} in the denominator. Therefore, any divergences are directly caused by degeneracies in the MO spectrum. To stabilize the optimization in such cases, we intervene in the gradient computation in Equation 6 with

1ϵi−ϵj↦{(ϵi−ϵj)−1,if ​|ϵi−ϵj|>δ0,otherwise.\frac{1}{\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}}\quad\mapsto\quad\begin{cases}(\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j})^{-1},&\text{if }|\epsilon_{i}-\epsilon_{j}|>\delta\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} (10)

We set δ=10−7​Ha\delta=10^{-7}\;\text{Ha} throughout. Any remaining optimization instability is removed by gradient clipping [1, 2]. Gradient clipping is considered standard numerical hygiene in artificial intelligence (AI) and Gaussian splat optimization in computer vision. In fact, our numerical tests indicate that gradient clipping is sufficient for reliable optimization at δ=0\delta=0.

Inverse Kohn-Sham

This subsection is devoted to relating the quantum Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence (or the von Neumann relative entropy) loss to the well-known Wu-Yang (WY) functional [3]. This derivation is presented in support of the point of view that the inverse Kohn-Sham (IKS) problem is fundamentally a supervised Hamiltonian learning problem. The goal of this learning task is to find the best single-particle potential vv by minimizing the quantum KL divergence

𝒟KL(ρ^0∥ρ^β[v])=−Tr⁡(ρ^0​(ln⁡ρ^β​[v]−ln⁡ρ^0))\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\rho}_{0}\parallel\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v])=-\Tr{ \Hat\rho_0 \left(\ln\Hat\rho_\beta[v] - \ln\Hat\rho_0 \right)} (11)

between the trial ρ^β​[v]\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v] and reference ρ^0\hat{\rho}_{0} density operators. Both are normalized states on the fermionic Fock space. The trial state can be reduced to the one-particle density matrix Γ⁡[v]=∑kfk​[v]​|ϕk​[v]⟩​⟨ϕk​[v]|\Gamma[v]=\sum_{k}f_{k}[v]\outerproduct*{\phi_k[v]}{\phi_k[v]} whose diagonal gives the trial density n⁡[v]n[v]. The orbitals are defined as the eigenstates of H^​[v]\hat{H}[v], represented in second quantization as

H^[v]=∫d3𝐫Ψ^†(𝐫)[−12∇2+v(𝐫)]Ψ^(𝐫)where{Ψ^(𝐫),Ψ^†(𝐫′)}=δ(𝐫−𝐫′)\hat{H}[v]=\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\left[-\tfrac{1}{2}\laplacian+v({\mathbf{r}})\right]\hat{\Psi}({\mathbf{r}})\qquad\text{where}\qquad\left\{\hat{\Psi}({\mathbf{r}}),\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\right\}=\delta({\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}) (12)

are the fermionic field operators. We set up our expressions in the grand-canonical ensemble, at finite inverse temperature β\beta and chemical potential μ\mu, with the intention of taking the limit β→∞\beta\rightarrow\infty as the final step. In the finite-temperature extension of DFT [4], we have

ρ^β​[v]=e−β​(H^​[v]−μ​N^)Z⁡[v;β,μ]andZ⁡[v;β,μ]=Tr⁡e−β​(H^​[v]−μ​N^)=e−β​Ω​[v;β,μ]\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v]=\frac{e^{-\beta(\hat{H}[v]-\mu\hat{N})}}{Z[v;\beta,\mu]}\qquad\text{and}\qquad Z[v;\beta,\mu]=\Tr e^{-\beta(\hat{H}[v]-\mu\hat{N})}=e^{-\beta\,\Omega[v;\beta,\mu]} (13)

defining the grand-canonical potential Ω=E−T​S−μ​N\Omega=E-TS-\mu N and the particle number operator N^=∫d3𝐫​Ψ^†​(𝐫)​Ψ^​(𝐫)\hat{N}=\int\differential[3]{\rr}\hat{\Psi}^{\dagger}({\mathbf{r}})\hat{\Psi}({\mathbf{r}}). This form of the density operator is the exponential family referred to in the main text, with −β​v-\beta v the natural parameter conjugate to the density nn. Defining

N0=Tr⁡(ρ^0​N^)andNβ​[v]=Tr⁡(ρ^β​[v]​N^)N_{0}=\Tr{\Hat\rho_0 \Hat N}\qquad\text{and}\qquad N_{\beta}[v]=\Tr{\Hat\rho_\beta[v] \Hat N} (14)

Equation 11 expands to the familiar free energy difference

𝒟KL(ρ^0∥ρ^β[v])=β[Tr⁡(ρ^0​H^​[v])−Tr⁡(ρ^β​[v]​H^​[v])−μ(N0−Nβ[v])]+S[ρ^β[v]]−S[ρ^0].\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\rho}_{0}\parallel\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v])=\;\beta\left[\Tr{\Hat\rho_0 \Hat H[v] }-\Tr{\Hat\rho_\beta[v] \Hat H[v]}-\mu\left(N_{0}-N_{\beta}[v]\right)\right]+S[\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v]]-S[\hat{\rho}_{0}]\;. (15)

We restrict the reference and trial states to the same expected particle number, N0=Nβ​[v]N_{0}=N_{\beta}[v], as in the fixed-NN KS problem. The chemical-potential term then vanishes. Although the relative entropy between distinct pure states may diverge as β→∞\beta\rightarrow\infty, its scaled limit is finite. If we decompose the trial Hamiltonian into kinetic and potential terms, we obtain

limβ→∞β−1𝒟KL(ρ^0∥ρ^β[v])=T0−Ts[ϕ[v]]+∫d3𝐫v(𝐫)(n0(𝐫)−n[v](𝐫)),\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}\beta^{-1}\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\rho}_{0}\parallel\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v])=T_{0}-T_{s}[\phi[v]]+\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;v({\mathbf{r}})\left(n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})-n[v]({\mathbf{r}})\right)\;, (16)

where T0=Tr⁡(ρ^0​T^)T_{0}=\Tr{\Hat\rho_0 \Hat T} is the kinetic energy of the reference state. This term does not contain any optimizable parameters and acts as an additive shift that vanishes under gradient optimization. If we drop the irrelevant constant, the resulting expression is precisely the negative of the well-known Wu-Yang functional [3]

W⁡[v]=Ts​[ϕ⁡[v]]+∫d3𝐫​v​(𝐫)​(n⁡[v]​(𝐫)−n0​(𝐫)),W[v]=T_{s}[\phi[v]]+\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;v({\mathbf{r}})\left(n[v]({\mathbf{r}})-n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\right)\;, (17)

which attains its maximal value for the exact IKS potential vv. Therefore,

argminvlimβ→∞β−1𝒟KL(ρ^0∥ρ^β[v])=argmaxvW[v].\argmin_{v}\lim_{\beta\rightarrow\infty}\beta^{-1}\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}}(\hat{\rho}_{0}\parallel\hat{\rho}_{\beta}[v])=\argmax_{v}W[v]\;. (18)

The connection between the quantum KL divergence and the WY functional can also be exploited to generalize the WY functional to finite-temperature density functional theory [4]. At finite β\beta, the potential-dependent part of −β−1​𝒟KL-\beta^{-1}\mathcal{D}_{\text{KL}} gives

Wβ​[v]=Es​[f⁡[v],ϕ⁡[v]]−T​S​[f⁡[v]]−∫d3𝐫​v​(𝐫)​n0​(𝐫),W_{\beta}[v]=E_{s}[f[v],\phi[v]]-TS[f[v]]-\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;v({\mathbf{r}})n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (19)

where Es​[f⁡[v],ϕ⁡[v]]−T​S​[f⁡[v]]E_{s}[f[v],\phi[v]]-TS[f[v]] is the KS free energy, Wβ​[v]W_{\beta}[v] reduces to W⁡[v]W[v] as β→∞\beta\rightarrow\infty, and

S[f]=−∑k(fklnfk+(1−fk)ln⁡(1−fk))withfk[v]=11+eβ​(ϵk​[v]−μ).S[f]=-\sum_{k}\left(f_{k}\ln f_{k}+(1-f_{k})\ln(1-f_k)\right)\qquad\text{with}\quad f_{k}[v]=\frac{1}{1+e^{\beta(\epsilon_{k}[v]-\mu)}}\;. (20)

To complete the optimization loop, we need functional gradients 𝛿W𝛿v\functionalderivative{W}{v} because they contribute to the energy gradients through ∂W⁡[v]∂θa=𝛿W⁡[v]𝛿v⋅∂v∂θa\partialderivative{W[v]}{\theta_a}=\functionalderivative{W[v]}{v}\cdot\partialderivative{v}{\theta_a}. Rewriting the WY functional using the total energy of the KS system as the sum of energies corresponding to occupied KS orbitals, we have

Ts​[ϕ]+∫d3𝐫​v​(𝐫)​n​(𝐫)=∑i=1Nϵi⇒W⁡[v]=∑i=1Nϵi​[v]−∫d3𝐫​v​(𝐫)​n0​(𝐫),T_{s}[\phi]+\int\differential[3]{\rr}v({\mathbf{r}})n({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}\quad\Rightarrow\quad W[v]=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\epsilon_{i}[v]-\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;v({\mathbf{r}})n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (21)

ready to exploit the perturbation theory result 𝛿ϵk𝛿v=|ϕk​(⋅)|2\functionalderivative{\epsilon_k}{v}=|\phi_{k}(\cdot)|^{2}. From there, by direct computation, we have

W⁡[v]=∑iϵi​[v]−∫d3𝐫​v​(𝐫)​n0​(𝐫)⇒𝛿W⁡[v]𝛿v=∑k|ϕk​(𝐫)|2−n0​(𝐫)=n⁡(𝐫)−n0​(𝐫).W[v]=\sum_{i}\epsilon_{i}[v]-\int\differential[3]{\rr}\;v({\mathbf{r}})n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\quad\Rightarrow\quad\functionalderivative{W[v]}{v}=\sum_{k}\left|\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\right|^{2}-n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})=n({\mathbf{r}})-n_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\;. (22)

The final gradient expression establishes two major advantages of the WY functional: it is concave with respect to the trial potential and the derivatives are simply given as local density residuals, bypassing the computation of excited states completely. Consequently, its negative defines a convex loss.

Supplementary Note 2: Regularization and null spaces

The proposed regularization function in the main text can be generalized to include a spatially dependent positive weight w⁡(𝐫)>0w({\mathbf{r}})>0,

R⁡[v]=18​π​∫d3𝐫​w​(𝐫)​|∇v​(𝐫)−∇v0​(𝐫)|2,R[v]=\frac{1}{8\pi}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\,w({\mathbf{r}})\,\left|\gradient v({\mathbf{r}})-\gradient v_{0}({\mathbf{r}})\right|^{2}\;, (23)

to regularize oscillations in some spatial regions more than others. In preparing this manuscript, we tried many different functional forms for ww, but none of them showed a decisive advantage over w=const.w=\text{const.} for all considered systems. In all cases, the regularization in Equation 23 is designed to select smooth potentials. This section is devoted to quantifying that statement. Let us assume for the moment that the optimization is carried out in functional space, free from finite parameterization artifacts. We restrict the analysis to a fixed-particle-number, vv-representable branch with a non-degenerate ground state, and assume that the implicit density functional E⁡[n]E[n] is locally twice differentiable. Inverse response operators are understood on the particle-conserving range after removing the constant-potential mode. Denoting the constrained total energy functional E⁡[v]=E⁡[ϕ⁡[v]]E[v]=E[\phi[v]], we construct a local quadratic approximation of the energy landscape:

E⁡[v+δ​v]=E⁡[v]+∫d3𝐫​𝛿E⁡[v]𝛿v⁡(𝐫)​δ​v​(𝐫)+12​∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​δ​v​(𝐫)​δ2​E​[v]δ​v​(𝐫)​δ​v​(𝐫′)​δ​v​(𝐫′)+𝒪⁡(δ​v3).E[v+\delta v]=E[v]+\int\differential[3]{\rr}\functionalderivative{E [v]}{v (\rr)}\delta v({\mathbf{r}})+\frac{1}{2}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\delta v({\mathbf{r}})\frac{\delta^{2}E[v]}{\delta v({\mathbf{r}})\delta v({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}\delta v({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})+\mathcal{O}(\delta v^{3})\;. (24)

At convergence, the linear term in Equation 24 vanishes because the exact OEP satisfies 𝛿E𝛿v=0\functionalderivative{E}{v}=0 by definition. Therefore, the stability is determined by the spectrum of the functional Hessian operator ℋ\mathcal{H}. Using δ2​Ts/δ​n2=−χs−1\delta^{2}T_{s}/\delta n^{2}=-\chi_{s}^{-1} on the restricted response space, we obtain

ℋ⁡(𝐫,𝐫′)=δ2​E​[v]δ​v​(𝐫)​δ​v​(𝐫′)=−χs​(𝐫,𝐫′)+∫d3𝐫1​∫d3𝐫2​χs​(𝐫,𝐫1)​𝒦Hxc​(𝐫1,𝐫2)​χs​(𝐫2,𝐫′),\mathcal{H}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\frac{\delta^{2}E[v]}{\delta v({\mathbf{r}})\delta v({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}=-\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})+\int\differential[3]{\rr_1}\int\differential[3]{\rr_2}\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}_{1})\mathcal{K}_{\text{Hxc}}({\mathbf{r}}_{1},{\mathbf{r}}_{2})\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}}_{2},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\;, (25)

or ℋ=−χs+χs​𝒦Hxc​χs\mathcal{H}=-\chi_{s}+\chi_{s}\mathcal{K}_{\text{Hxc}}\chi_{s} in the terse operator notation, with the Kohn-Sham response defined as χs=𝛿n𝛿v\chi_{s}=\functionalderivative{n}{v}, and the Hartree-exchange-correlation (HXC) kernel as

𝒦Hxc​(𝐫,𝐫′)=1|𝐫−𝐫′|+δ2​Excδ​n​(𝐫)​δ​n​(𝐫′).\mathcal{K}_{\text{Hxc}}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\frac{1}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}+\frac{\delta^{2}E_{\text{xc}}}{\delta n({\mathbf{r}})\delta n({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}\;. (26)

Because v=vext+vHxcv=v_{\text{ext}}+v_{\text{Hxc}} at convergence, we have a clean connection with the total response χ=𝛿n𝛿vext\chi=\functionalderivative{n}{v_\ext}

𝒦Hxc=χs−1−χ−1⇒ℋ=−χs​χ−1​χs,\mathcal{K}_{\text{Hxc}}=\chi_{s}^{-1}-\chi^{-1}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathcal{H}=-\chi_{s}\chi^{-1}\chi_{s}\;, (27)

where we have used Equation 25. At a stable ground state, χ\chi is negative definite on the restricted response space. Therefore, for any potential perturbation δ​v\delta v,

δ​v⊤​ℋ​δ​v=−(χs​δ​v)⊤​χ−1​(χs​δ​v)≥0,\delta v^{\top}\mathcal{H}\delta v=-(\chi_{s}\delta v)^{\top}\chi^{-1}(\chi_{s}\delta v)\geq 0, (28)

with equality holding if and only if χs​δ​v=0\chi_{s}\delta v=0. Hence, ℋ\mathcal{H} and χs\chi_{s} share the same null space under the assumptions stated above. In the complete functional formulation, the static response has only the constant-potential zero mode for a non-degenerate ground state, consistent with the Hohenberg-Kohn uniqueness theorem [5]. In a finite orbital basis, additional potential perturbations can be invisible to the finite orbital-product space [6]. If the tangent space of vθv_{\theta} contains such perturbations, the null space is artificially expanded to include highly oscillatory functions φ\varphi for which χs​φ=ℋ​φ=0\chi_{s}\varphi=\mathcal{H}\varphi=0.

Any such parameterization, linear or nonlinear, induces a tangent space basis expansion of the form

δ​v​(𝐫)↦δ​vθ​(𝐫)=∑μ∂vθ​(𝐫)∂θμ​δ​θμ,\delta v({\mathbf{r}})\quad\mapsto\quad\delta v_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{\mu}\partialderivative{v_\theta(\rr)}{\theta^\mu}\delta\theta^{\mu}\;, (29)

where φμ​(𝐫)=∂vθ​(𝐫)∂θμ\varphi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})=\partialderivative{v_\theta(\rr)}{\theta^\mu} are thought of as basis functions indexed by μ\mu and δ​θμ\delta\theta^{\mu} as the expansion coefficients. The expansion in Equation 29 combines with the Hessian Equation 24 to project the Hessian operator into the tangent space basis at convergence or self-consistency

ℋ↦ℋμ​ν=φμ⊤​ℋ​φν=−(χs​φμ)⊤​χ−1​(χs​φν),\mathcal{H}\quad\mapsto\quad\mathcal{H}_{\mu\nu}=\varphi_{\mu}^{\top}\mathcal{H}\varphi_{\nu}=-(\chi_{s}\varphi_{\mu})^{\top}\chi^{-1}(\chi_{s}\varphi_{\nu})\;, (30)

in operator notation, deployed to avoid quadruple integrals. For a nonlinear parameterization, the exact parameter Hessian contains an additional curvature term,

∂2E∂θμ​∂θν=ℋμ​ν+∫d3𝐫​𝛿E𝛿v⁡(𝐫)​∂2vθ​(𝐫)∂θμ​∂θν.\partialderivative{E}{\theta^\mu}{\theta^\nu}=\mathcal{H}_{\mu\nu}+\int\differential[3]{\rr}\,\functionalderivative{E}{v(\rr)}\partialderivative{v_\theta(\rr)}{\theta^\mu}{\theta^\nu}\;. (31)

The extra term in Equation 31 vanishes at the functional stationary point assumed above. Away from that point, Equation 29 gives the pullback of the functional Hessian rather than the complete parameter Hessian. As noted in the main text, we optimize a regularized energy expression. Therefore, the Hessian operator introduced by Equation 24 needs to be supplemented with the Hessian of Equation 23,

ℋ(R)(𝐫,𝐫′)=δ2​R​[v]δ​v​(𝐫)​δ​v​(𝐫′)=−14​π∇⁣⋅(w(𝐫)∇δ(𝐫−𝐫′)),\mathcal{H}^{(R)}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\frac{\delta^{2}R[v]}{\delta v({\mathbf{r}})\delta v({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}=-\frac{1}{4\pi}\divergence\left(w({\mathbf{r}})\,\gradient\delta({\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\right)\;, (32)

yielding its finite-basis form

ℋμ​ν(R)=14​π∫d3𝐫w(𝐫)∇φμ(𝐫)⋅∇φν(𝐫),\mathcal{H}^{(R)}_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{4\pi}\int\differential[3]{\rr}w({\mathbf{r}})\;\gradient\varphi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})\cdot\gradient\varphi_{\nu}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (33)

after simplification by partial integration. If w⁡(𝐫)w({\mathbf{r}}) is positive everywhere, its quadratic form is strictly positive for every non-constant potential perturbation. The matrix in Equation 33 is therefore positive definite when the tangent functions {φμ}\{\varphi_{\mu}\} are linearly independent, up to constant shifts. The regularized total energy Hessian operator at convergence reads

ℋtot=−∫d3𝐫1∫d3𝐫2χs(𝐫,𝐫1)χ−1(𝐫1,𝐫2)χs(𝐫2,𝐫′)−λ4​π∇⁣⋅(w(𝐫)∇δ(𝐫−𝐫′)).\mathcal{H}_{\text{tot}}=-\int\differential[3]{\rr_1}\int\differential[3]{\rr_2}\;\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}_{1})\chi^{-1}({\mathbf{r}}_{1},{\mathbf{r}}_{2})\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}}_{2},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})-\frac{\lambda}{4\pi}\divergence\left(w({\mathbf{r}})\,\gradient\delta({\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})\right)\;. (34)

At a local minimum, the unregularized Hessian is positive semidefinite. The total Hessian is therefore positive definite on the gauge-fixed potential tangent space as long as λ​w​(𝐫)>0\lambda w({\mathbf{r}})>0 and the parameterization contains no redundant tangent directions.

Supplementary Note 3: Multipole splat parameterization

As noted in the main text, optimizable parameters θ\theta consist of individual multipole parameters – monopole charges qkq_{k}, dipole moments 𝐩k\mathbf{p}_{k} as well as positions 𝐚k\mathbf{a}_{k} and exponents αk\alpha_{k}. For completeness, the total variational potential can be written down as an electrostatic Coulomb potential

vθ​(𝐫)=∫d3𝐫′​ρθ​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|v_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}})=\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\,\frac{\rho_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|} (35)

sourced by a charge density

ρθ​(𝐫)=ρext​(𝐫)+N−1N​nref​(𝐫)+∑kqk​ρk​(𝐫)−∑k𝐩k⋅∇ρk​(𝐫),\rho_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}})=\rho_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})+\tfrac{N-1}{N}n_{\text{ref}}({\mathbf{r}})+\sum_{k}q_{k}\rho_{k}({\mathbf{r}})-\sum_{k}\mathbf{p}_{k}\cdot\gradient\rho_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (36)

where nrefn_{\text{ref}} is the reference (Hartree-Fock) density and

ρext(𝐫)=−∑aZaδ(𝐫−𝐑a);ρk(𝐫)=(αkπ)3/2e−αk​|𝐫−𝐚k|2.\rho_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})=-\sum_{a}Z_{a}\delta({\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{R}}_{a})\;;\qquad\rho_{k}({\mathbf{r}})=\left(\frac{\alpha_{k}}{\pi}\right)^{\nicefrac{{3}}{{2}}}e^{-\alpha_{k}|{\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{a}_{k}|^{2}}\;. (37)

Terms in Equation 36 separate the analytically known static nuclear contribution in the first term from the precomputed Fermi-Amaldi (FA) background in the second term. The source density in Equation 36 generates the Coulomb potential

vθ​(𝐫)=vext​(𝐫)+vFA​(𝐫)+∑kqk​vk​(𝐫)−∑k𝐩k⋅∇vk​(𝐫),v_{\theta}({\mathbf{r}})=v_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})+v_{\text{FA}}({\mathbf{r}})+\sum_{k}q_{k}v_{k}({\mathbf{r}})-\sum_{k}\mathbf{p}_{k}\cdot\gradient v_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\;, (38)

where

vext(𝐫)=−∑aZa|𝐫−𝐑a|,vFA(𝐫)=N−1N∫d3𝐫′nref​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|andvk(𝐫)=erf⁡(αk​|𝐫−𝐚k|)|𝐫−𝐚k|.v_{\text{ext}}({\mathbf{r}})=-\sum_{a}\frac{Z_{a}}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{R}}_{a}|}\;,\qquad v_{\text{FA}}({\mathbf{r}})=\frac{N-1}{N}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\,\frac{n_{\text{ref}}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}\qquad\text{and}\qquad v_{k}({\mathbf{r}})=\frac{\erf(\sqrt{\alpha_k} |\rr- \vb a _k|)}{|{\mathbf{r}}-\mathbf{a}_{k}|}\;. Analytically transitioning from Equation 36 to Equation 38 is made possible by convenient integral identities,

or by making use of Gauss’ law for the spherically-symmetric Gaussian charge distribution ρk\rho_{k}.

The only physical constraint on the parameters is the restriction on the total charge to lock in the asymptotic decay of both the source density and the potential. As noted in the main text, for N1N_{1} monopoles, we set

Dipole moments 𝐩\mathbf{p} are directly optimized as they do not contribute to the total charge and cannot ruin the asymptotics.

Multipole positions and Gaussian exponents are parameterized in a way that restricts their values in the environment of nuclei at coordinates 𝐑a{\mathbf{R}}_{a} with charges ZaZ_{a}. Each multipole position 𝐚\mathbf{a} is modeled as

𝐚=𝐀+RT​tanh⁡(|𝐛−𝐀|RT)​𝐛−𝐀|𝐛−𝐀|\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{A}+R_{T}\,\tanh\left(\frac{|\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}|}{R_{T}}\right)\;\frac{\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}}{|\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{A}|} (42)

and unconstrained vector 𝐛\mathbf{b}. The point of Equation 42 is to prevent multipoles from drifting too far away from the nuclei, spoiling the asymptotic behavior in practice. During optimization, they are allowed to exit the interatomic region at most one tube radius RTR_{T} away from its anchor point 𝐀\mathbf{A}. We set RT=η​dmaxR_{T}=\eta d_{\text{max}} where η=0.8\eta=0.8 and

dmax={maxa,b⁡|𝐑a−𝐑b|,if ​Natm>1RvdW,if ​Natm=1d_{\text{max}}=\begin{cases}\max_{a,b}|{\mathbf{R}}_{a}-{\mathbf{R}}_{b}|,&\text{if }N_{\text{atm}}>1\\ R_{\text{vdW}},&\text{if }N_{\text{atm}}=1\end{cases} (44)

is the largest geometric length scale in the molecule with NatmN_{\text{atm}} atoms or the van der Waals radius RvdWR_{\text{vdW}} of a single atom.

α=αmin×(αmaxαmin)s⁡(x)wheres⁡(x)=11+e−x.\alpha=\alpha_{\text{min}}\times\left(\frac{\alpha_{\text{max}}}{\alpha_{\text{min}}}\right)^{s(x)}\qquad\text{where}\qquad s(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\;. (45)

The per-splat exponent bounds are automatically assigned at initialization as αmin=(2​Lmax2)−1\alpha_{\text{min}}=(2L_{\text{max}}^{2})^{-1} and αmax=4​Zeff2\alpha_{\text{max}}=4Z_{\text{eff}}^{2}, where Zeff,k=∑a𝒜k​a​ZaZ_{\text{eff},k}=\sum_{a}\mathcal{A}_{ka}Z_{a} and

Lmax=max⁡(RvdW,2​ℓx2+ℓy2+ℓz2),L_{\text{max}}=\max\left(R_{\text{vdW}},2\sqrt{\ell_{x}^{2}+\ell_{y}^{2}+\ell_{z}^{2}}\right)\;, (46)

with ℓi2=Varp𝐑a,i\ell^{2}_{i}=\Var_{p}{\mathbf{R}}_{a,i} being the charge-weighted variance of nuclear positions with respect to the normalized distribution pa∝Zap_{a}\propto Z_{a}. After initialization, the exponent bounds are frozen and treated as constants during optimization.

Physical initialization of multipole positions reduces the number of optimization steps that need to be taken. We exploit access to spatial profiles of converged reference orbitals (Hartree-Fock in all studied systems) to construct localized orbitals. Using the Boys localization procedure, we construct localized φk\varphi_{k} as the minimizer of the variance of the position operator 𝐫^\hat{\mathbf{r}},

ℒBoys=∑l[⟨φl|​𝐫^2​|φl⟩−⟨φl|​𝐫^​|φl⟩2].\mathcal{L}_{\text{Boys}}=\sum_{l}\left[\bra{\varphi_l}\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{2}\ket{\varphi_l}-\bra{\varphi_l}\hat{\mathbf{r}}\ket{\varphi_l}^{2}\right]\;. (47)

Optimizing Equation 47 ensures that the localized orbitals have minimal spatial extent. Individual real-space means 𝝁l=⟨φl|​𝐫^​|φl⟩\bm{\mu}_{l}=\bra{\varphi_l}\hat{\mathbf{r}}\ket{\varphi_l} and variances σl2=⟨φl|​𝐫^2​|φl⟩−⟨φl|​𝐫^​|φl⟩2\sigma_{l}^{2}=\bra{\varphi_l}\hat{\mathbf{r}}^{2}\ket{\varphi_l}-\bra{\varphi_l}\hat{\mathbf{r}}\ket{\varphi_l}^{2} are a natural byproduct of the Boys optimization. We use 𝝁l\bm{\mu}_{l} and σl\sigma_{l} to initialize the Gaussian positions 𝐚\mathbf{a} and exponents α\alpha. For NsplatN_{\text{splat}} splats and NorbN_{\text{orb}} states, each localized orbital is allocated Nsplat/NorbN_{\text{splat}}/N_{\text{orb}} splats. For a given splat kk assigned to orbital ll, we set

𝐚k=𝝁l+σl​𝐳andαk=eκ​u2​σl2;\mathbf{a}_{k}=\bm{\mu}_{l}+\sigma_{l}\,\mathbf{z}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\alpha_{k}=\frac{e^{\kappa u}}{2\sigma_{l}^{2}}\;; (48)

where κ=1\kappa=1, 𝐳∼𝒩⁡(0,𝟙)\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\mathbbm{1}), and u∼𝒩⁡(0,1)u\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1) are sampled independently for each multipole. Initialization according to Equation 48 ensures that positions have a normal distribution around the centers of localized orbitals while widths are distributed according to the log-normal distribution to cover several orders of magnitude around the localized orbital width.

In small systems with one or two electrons, the Boys initialization would initialize all splats in one point or a narrow region. In those cases, we default to initializing all splat positions by assigning a fixed fraction of all splats to each atom aa, and sampling the final position from a Gaussian centered at that atom, with width set to a fixed fraction of its vdW radius RvdW,aR_{\text{vdW},a}: 𝐚∼𝒩⁡(𝐑a,ξ2​RvdW,a2​𝟙)\mathbf{a}\sim\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{R}}_{a},\xi^{2}R_{\text{vdW},a}^{2}\mathbbm{1}), with ξ=0.8\xi=0.8.

Supplementary Note 4: Comparison with other exact exchange solvers

In the traditional exact exchange (EXX) literature, the finite-basis expansion of the potential is modeled as an implicit density functional, in order to fit into the self-consistent field (SCF) framework. As noted in the main text, this density functional is evaluated by inverting the KS density response function χs=𝛿n𝛿v\chi_{s}=\functionalderivative{n}{v}, introducing numerical stability issues. However, formally, the potential can be evaluated as a solution to a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind. In the operator language, this equation can concisely be derived by careful application of the chain rule of functional derivatives,

𝛿Exc𝛿n=𝛿Exc𝛿v⋅𝛿v𝛿n⇒𝛿n𝛿v⋅𝛿Exc𝛿n=𝛿Exc𝛿v⇔∫d3𝐫′χs(𝐫,𝐫′)vxc(𝐫′)=𝛿Exc𝛿v⁡(𝐫).\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{n}=\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{v}\cdot\functionalderivative{v}{n}\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\functionalderivative{n}{v}\cdot\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{n}=\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{v}\qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\;\chi_{s}({\mathbf{r}},{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})v_{\text{xc}}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})=\functionalderivative{E_\xc}{v (\rr)}\;. (49)

It is natural to represent the potential vxcv_{\text{xc}} in an auxiliary basis and attempt to invert the resulting matrix. When interfaced with a standard self-consistent field relaxation, one such linear solve is required per iteration. For completeness, we state the finite-basis implicit exchange functional evaluation here. For an orbital basis expansion |ϕk⟩=∑μCμ​k​|χμ⟩\ket*{\phi_k}=\sum_{\mu}C_{\mu k}\ket*{\chi_\mu} coupled with an auxiliary basis potential expansion vx​(𝐫)=∑αvα​φα​(𝐫)v_{\text{x}}({\mathbf{r}})=\sum_{\alpha}v_{\alpha}\varphi_{\alpha}({\mathbf{r}}), the potential basis functions are generated by source densities ρα\rho_{\alpha} as φα​(𝐫)=∫d3𝐫′​ρα​(𝐫′)/|𝐫−𝐫′|\varphi_{\alpha}({\mathbf{r}})=\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\,\rho_{\alpha}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})/|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|. We have the linear system X​𝐯=𝐭X\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{t} where

Xα​β=∑k∈occ∑l∈virtDk​l,α1ϵk−ϵlDk​l,βandtα=−∑k∈occ∑l∈virtDk​l,α1ϵk−ϵl⟨ϕk|K|ϕl⟩X_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{k\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{l\in\mathrm{virt}}D_{kl,\alpha}\frac{1}{\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon_{l}}D_{kl,\beta}\qquad\text{and}\qquad t_{\alpha}=-\sum_{k\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{l\in\mathrm{virt}}D_{kl,\alpha}\frac{1}{\epsilon_{k}-\epsilon_{l}}\bra{\phi_k}K\ket{\phi_l} (50)

with Dk​l,αD_{kl,\alpha} related to the standard three-center integrals (μ​ν|α)(\mu\nu|\alpha) commonly evaluated in density fitting routines

Dk​l,α=∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​ϕk​(𝐫)​ϕl​(𝐫)​ρα​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|=∑μ​νCμ​k​Cν​l​∫d3𝐫​∫d3𝐫′​χμ​(𝐫)​χν​(𝐫)​ρα​(𝐫′)|𝐫−𝐫′|=∑μ​νCμ​k​Cν​l​(μ​ν|α)D_{kl,\alpha}=\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{\phi_{k}({\mathbf{r}})\phi_{l}({\mathbf{r}})\rho_{\alpha}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}=\sum_{\mu\nu}C_{\mu k}C_{\nu l}\int\differential[3]{\rr}\int\differential[3]{\rr'}\frac{\chi_{\mu}({\mathbf{r}})\chi_{\nu}({\mathbf{r}})\rho_{\alpha}({\mathbf{r}}^{\prime})}{|{\mathbf{r}}-{\mathbf{r}}^{\prime}|}=\sum_{\mu\nu}C_{\mu k}C_{\nu l}(\mu\nu|\alpha) (51)

and KK is the positive exchange operator defined in Supplementary Note 1: Exact gradients, so the nonlocal exchange contribution to the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian is −K-K.

The naive unregularized approach, simply evaluating 𝐯x=X−1​𝐭\mathbf{v}_{\text{x}}=X^{-1}\mathbf{t}, is not stable numerically, as the matrix is ill-conditioned for two independent reasons:

  • •

    Finite auxiliary basis artifacts: Finite basis expansion grows the null space of the KS from just all constant shifts of the potential to many highly oscillatory functions that are nearly orthogonal to the orbital-product space. They carry low weight in the singular value decomposition of XX, but get amplified in the inverse matrix X−1X^{-1}.

  • •

    Orbital and auxiliary basis mismatch: Coupling an insufficient auxiliary basis with a large orbital basis (or vice-versa) can result in convergence to unphysical potentials that optimize expressivity gaps instead of physical features.

We show the resulting unphysical potential for illustrative purposes on Figure 1, after just one exact inversion starting from the converged Hartree-Fock (HF) orbitals.

Trushin and Görling (TG) [9, 10] have introduced a physically principled and numerically stable auxiliary basis preprocessing approach that mitigates both classes of problems. They eliminate basis functions that violate the target −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} asymptotics before starting the SCF procedure, while giving recommended basis pairs and a default value for the response matrix singular value cutoff. Their approach comes in two variants: the "bare" approach described above and a version that additionally enforces the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) condition

⟨ϕHOMO|​v^x​|ϕHOMO⟩=⟨ϕHOMO|​v^xNL​|ϕHOMO⟩\bra{\phi_\text{HOMO}}\hat{v}_{\text{x}}\ket{\phi_\text{HOMO}}=\bra{\phi_\text{HOMO}}\hat{v}_{\text{x}}^{\text{NL}}\ket{\phi_\text{HOMO}} (52)

in preprocessing the auxiliary potential basis. In Equation 52, v^x\hat{v}_{\text{x}} is the KS exchange potential operator and v^xNL\hat{v}_{\text{x}}^{\text{NL}} is the non-local (Hartree-Fock) exchange potential formed with KS orbitals. Both variants of the TG approach have allowed the auxiliary-basis OEP to be applied to a wider range of systems.

The HOMO condition is specific to EXX. It is recovered by a complete OEP solution but need not be satisfied in finite orbital and potential representations. Ref. [9] enforces it explicitly during auxiliary-basis preprocessing in a variant of their approach (TG-HC), while the Krieger-Li-Iafrate (KLI) semi-analytical potential [7, 8] fixes the corresponding highest-occupied shift by construction. HF retains the nonlocal exchange operator and is not a local potential calculation. Multipole splat potentials instead enforce the exchange charge condition and the resulting −1/r\nicefrac{{-1}}{{r}} asymptote. We do not impose Equation 52 because it has no simple analogue for correlation potentials, while the present framework targets general orbital-dependent functionals. Agreement with the real-space HOMO levels is an independent benchmark for our calculations precisely because no HOMO eigenvalue or other spectral target enters the optimization. Therefore, the bare TG calculation is the closest methodological comparison.

In Table 1, we compare the results of multipole splat direct optimization to both variants of the TG approach using the recommended aug-cc-pwCVQZ orbital basis. We compare the negative HOMO eigenvalues −ϵHOMO-\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}} and total EXX energies using the numerical values reported in Ref. [9]. We use atomic systems where accurate EXX reference HOMO eigenvalues are available, calculated on real-space grids by TG as well using the RELKS code [11, 12, 13].

Values sufficiently close (∼10\sim 10 mHa) to the Hartree-Fock value are a necessary but not sufficient condition for retrieving the physical exchange potential. Multipole splat potentials produce energies of the correct magnitude.

Another necessary condition is an accurate HOMO eigenvalue. For the EXX model, the real-space reference values provide an independent spectral benchmark. For all five atoms with available reference values, the multipole-splat HOMO eigenvalue is closer to the reference than the bare TG result. The mean absolute deviations are 7.17.1 mHa for MS and 25.325.3 mHa for TG. This comparison should not be interpreted as a general ranking of the methods: TG-HC explicitly enforces the EXX HOMO condition, KLI satisfies the corresponding condition by construction, and HF retains the nonlocal exchange operator. The MS values emerge without direct HOMO enforcement.

We supplement numerical comparisons on atomic systems with a visual comparison of potential profiles in molecular systems in Figure 1 against the KLI potential for CO and SiO molecules presented in the main text. We see that the multipole splat potentials produce smooth potentials with sharp physical features.

Supplementary Note 5: Hyperparameter ablations

In this section, we present the results of hyperparameter ablations for the multipole splat EXX OEP and IKS. We vary the splat monopole counts N1N_{1}, splat dipole counts N2N_{2}, the size of orbital basis as X in aug-cc-pVXZ and the regularization parameter λ\lambda. Potentials are compared in real-space plots as well as through localization energies and total variation between OEP and reference densities.

Our main findings are:

  • •

    Converged potential profiles are visually indistinguishable across a factor of eight in splat count. All three diagnostics (the HOMO eigenvalue, the localization energy, and the density total variation) are essentially flat over this range.

  • •

    As noted in the main text, localization energies are a non-monotonically moving target with respect to a growing orbital basis. They rise monotonically within each basis family, but adding core-valence functions raises ElocE_{\text{loc}} enough that its value at cT exceeds the one at Q, and cQ exceeds 5. Neither ϵHOMO\epsilon_{\text{HOMO}} nor 𝒟TV\mathcal{D}_{\text{TV}} inherits this sawtooth pattern, both staying within a narrow band from triple-zeta onward. The double-zeta basis is the only one departing appreciably from the converged potential shape, underestimating the depth of the core wells.

  • •

    All three diagnostics display the expected elbow-like behavior with respect to the regularization parameter λ\lambda. They remain unchanged for λ≲2.5×10−4\lambda\lesssim 2.5\times 10^{-4}, degrading only once the regularizer starts to compete with the primary objective at λ≈10−2\lambda\approx 10^{-2}. The Pareto-optimal λ\lambda can be fine-tuned to this elbow for each molecule for added control over regularization effects.

  • •

    Lowering λ\lambda below ∼2.5×10−5\sim 2.5\times 10^{-5} sharpens the core wells and intershell features slightly. However, the textbook OEP oscillations are suppressed even at lowest values of λ≈2.5×10−7\lambda\approx 2.5\times 10^{-7}.

Diagnostics are shown in Figure 2 and the corresponding converged potential profiles in Figure 3.

Supplementary Note 6: Additional numerical details and potential profiles

Common numerical details

Common hyperparameters of all calculations reported in the main text are collected in Table 2.

Comments on individual hyperparameters:

  • •

    CCSD(T) reference: For all IKS calculations, we use a relaxed CCSD(T) reference density computed in the same orbital basis and with the same restricted spatial-orbital convention as the inversion. The spin-summed one-particle reduced density matrix in the atomic-orbital basis is passed directly to the IKS optimization. All CCSD(T) calculations were carried out using PySCF [14, 15].

  • •

    Regularization (λ\lambda): The tabulated value is the exact-exchange value. Hybrid functionals (B3LYP, PBE0) scale λ\lambda by the exact-exchange fraction γ\gamma (0.200.20 and 0.250.25). CCSD(T) inversion (IKS) uses the EXX γ=1\gamma=1 value.

  • •

    Optimizer and schedule: The quoted learning rate is the peak of a cosine one-cycle schedule (Adamax, global gradient-norm clip 1.01.0). An exponential moving average of the parameters with decay 0.990.99 is applied except where noted.

  • •

    Spin/occupation: All calculations are spin-restricted, with a single shared spatial-orbital set and occupations in {0,1,2}\{0,1,2\}.

Specific comments for individual systems and calculations:

  1. 1.

    Small systems: Point-group symmetrization was used for atoms and symmetric linear molecules.

  2. 2.

    Dissociation: Atom-Gaussian initialization was used instead of Boys localization, which is unreliable for one- and two-electron systems or stretched bonds. Grid level 5 and wide splat exponent bounds, 10−3<α<10410^{-3}<\alpha<10^{4}, were used. The basis is aug-cc-pwCV5Z where available, with aug-cc-pV5Z used for the H and He curves. H+2{}_{2}^{+} is a doublet (Nα−Nβ=1N_{\alpha}-N_{\beta}=1, or spin=1 in PySCF), and its CCSD(T) inversion runs without density fitting.

  3. 3.

    Rydberg: A custom diffuse Ne basis (Table 3) was coupled with an extended radial grid (per-element radial scaling ×5\times 5, grid level 5). An enlarged splat tube radius (tube scale 3.653.65) and wide exponent bounds, 10−4<α<10410^{-4}<\alpha<10^{4}, were used.

  4. 4.

    GW100: The subset was restricted to molecules with N≤40N\leq 40 electrons. Fewer optimization steps (4000) were used for affordability across the set.

  5. 5.

    Larger systems: A non-augmented basis and reduced integration grid were used. The splats were initialized with C6C_{6} symmetry for benzene and D2​hD_{2h} symmetry for naphthalene.

Reference spectral data processing

Reference term values are taken from the Ne I level list in the NIST Atomic Spectra Database [16]. Ne I series converge to the two spin-orbit components of the Ne+ core, 2​s2​2​p5​P3/2∘22s^{2}2p^{5}\,{}^{2}P^{\circ}_{3/2} and 2​s2​2​p5​P1/2∘22s^{2}2p^{5}\,{}^{2}P^{\circ}_{1/2}. We use the lower ionization limit, IP=0.7924823I_{P}=0.7924823 Ha, corresponding to 2​s2​2​p5​P3/2∘22s^{2}2p^{5}\,{}^{2}P^{\circ}_{3/2}. Each nominal n​sns or n​dnd member splits into several fine-structure levels. We do not average these levels, but retain one consistently labeled branch of each series:

  • •

    n​sns: 2s22p5(P3/2∘2)ns[3/2]1∘22s^{2}2p^{5}({}^{2}P^{\circ}_{3/2})ns\,{}^{2}[3/2]^{\circ}_{1};

  • •

    n​dnd: 2s22p5(P3/2∘2)nd[3/2]1∘22s^{2}2p^{5}({}^{2}P^{\circ}_{3/2})nd\,{}^{2}[3/2]^{\circ}_{1}.

These are the J=1J=1, odd-parity branches in NIST’s Racah notation and are dipole allowed from the S01{}^{1}S_{0} ground state. All other fine-structure levels and the series converging to the upper P1/2∘2{}^{2}P^{\circ}_{1/2} core limit are excluded. NIST gives the term values EnE_{n} relative to the Ne ground state. We convert them to the KS eigenvalue convention by

εnNIST=EnNIST−IP,\varepsilon_{n}^{\text{NIST}}=E_{n}^{\text{NIST}}-I_{P}, (53)

so that εnNIST<0\varepsilon_{n}^{\text{NIST}}<0 for every bound member and εnNIST→0−\varepsilon_{n}^{\text{NIST}}\to 0^{-} as n→∞n\to\infty, consistent with the sign convention used for our own OEP virtual eigenvalues. Quantum defects are extracted by inverting the Rydberg formula,

μl=n−12​|εnNIST|,\mu_{l}=n-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2|\varepsilon_{n}^{\text{NIST}}|}}\;, (54)

evaluated separately for each series member. The defect remains member-dependent at low nn. The values reported in the main text are obtained from an unweighted one-parameter least-squares fit of the Rydberg formula to the selected n=3n=3–66 term values,

μl=argminμ∑n=36[εnNIST+12​(n−μ)2]2.\mu_{l}=\argmin_{\mu}\sum_{n=3}^{6}\left[\varepsilon_{n}^{\text{NIST}}+\frac{1}{2(n-\mu)^{2}}\right]^{2}\;. (55)

This gives μs=1.331\mu_{s}=1.331 and μd=0.012\mu_{d}=0.012. No n→∞n\to\infty extrapolation or averaging over fine-structure levels is used.

The Ne Rydberg calculations use a customized orbital basis: the standard aug-cc-pVQZ set for neon, augmented with six additional single-primitive diffuse shells in each of the ss, pp, and dd angular momenta. Rydberg orbitals are hydrogenic and spatially extended. The n​sns or n​dnd series up to n≈6n\approx 6 samples regions tens of Bohr from the nucleus, so they require Gaussians with exponents far smaller than those provided by valence-optimized sets. Each added series continues the geometric progression already present in the parent basis. Starting from the most diffuse exponent of that angular momentum in aug-cc-pVQZ (0.10540.1054, 0.08180.0818, 0.27300.2730 a.u. for ss, pp, dd, respectively), successive exponents are generated by repeated division by 33 (six times), reaching ∼10−4\sim 10^{-4} a.u. Continuing the existing even-tempered series keeps the added shells smoothly spaced and reduces the risk of near-linear dependence relative to an ad hoc overcomplete set. The extended basis is paired with an extended radial DFT grid (per-element radial scaling ×5\times 5, grid level 5) and an enlarged splat tube radius (tube scale 3.653.65), so that both the orbitals and the optimized effective potential have the spatial support needed to bind the Rydberg states. Numerical values of the additional exponents are listed in Table 3.

Additional potential profiles

Localization energies and density total variations are reported in Table 4. Corresponding converged potentials for the remaining systems studied in this work are collected in Figure 4.

The B3LYP and PBE0 potentials in Figure 4 are nearly indistinguishable from one another throughout. Atomic and molecular shell structure is resolved as intershell shoulders and bond-region plateaus. The profiles show no visible numerical noise except for a peak inversion in Be2, which also requires special treatment in other OEP approaches [9].
